That was until she recently came across the organisation School Can't Australia on social media and decided to attend an online forum.

"I said, 'I hope you don't mind my being here; I'm not a parent, I'm actually someone who didn't go to school'."

Judith said that with the help of School Can't Australia, she finally started to understand herself and to feel understood by others.

Judith went on to attain a PhD and teach Latin and ancient Greek. (ABC News: Armin Azad)

From repeated absences to PhD

Judith's inability to attend school caused friction between her parents, with one supporting her staying at home while the other fretted about her lack of socialisation.

She was not averse to learning and said she spent much of high school at home in her pyjamas, reading novels.

"Then I started teaching myself piano, started teaching myself Latin," she said.

She repeated some years and eventually went on to university — as a student and then as a lecturer, in Australia and abroad.

" I reckon I went to school half of my 14 years … I have a PhD, and I teach Latin and ancient Greek. "

School Can't Australia director Tiffany Westphal said that while Judith's school struggles may have occurred a long time ago, the causes today were still much the same.

While being made a "dunce" was a thing of the past, she said children still experienced classroom shame.

A letter from Judith's principal to her parents in December 1973. (Supplied)

"Sometimes it happens in reverse; instead of being punished, people are rewarded. You get your name up on the board if you've done well.

"But if you're the kid who never gets their name on the board … that can impress on a young person just as significantly as being publicly shamed."

Ms Westphal said Judith's self-consciousness about her eczema was also relatable to many of today's students.

"The impact of being different and having this different need for care … how that makes you feel a bit different from your peers," she said.

" Sometimes those needs are understood and sometimes they're not. "

Never too late to focus on education

Judith has some regrets about the impact not going to school had on her socially.

"I was so isolated, particularly as a teenager when my parents weren't spending so much time with me at home," she said.

" It's taken me a long time to become more comfortable in a public sphere. "

She said she had no regrets about her low attendance from an academic viewpoint.

"If you want to do something, you just work around to find out how you do it, even if you didn't have the best start at the typical route," she said.

"I've had students who were middle-aged, hadn't done any more years at school than they were required to, got married and had children, and then went to uni."

Ms Westphal said many "school can't" families in Australia today were having to experiment with their child's education.

"There's a lot of narrative at schools about how the way you finish your education, those last couple of years at school, really writes your future, but it doesn't," she said.

"There are so many other pathways.

"When people find the thing that gives them joy or makes their heart sing, something that they can get their teeth into and feel good about, they can do amazing things in learning."

As Judith got older, anxiety overtook allergies as her main reason for not attending classes. (ABC News)

Courage to go to school could take 'several days'

Judith's advice to parents today: don't tackle the issue on a school morning.

"One thing I never explained to my parents was that it could take me several days of gearing my courage up, girding my loins, to think that I'm going to be able to attend school.

"So if my parents were then trying to get me to go to school on the morning of the school day, it was just far too late.

"I would have decided the night before whether I was ready or not.

" It's very important to talk about the issue in a calm manner at a time when it's not crucial how the conversation goes. "

Judith was a "school can't" child in the 1960s and 70s. (ABC News: Armin Azad)

Judith said it was nice to see more support in place for today's "school can't" kids, with options for online learning and more opportunities for social engagement.

"There's more awareness of the problems that children can have, psychological problems of one sort and another," she said.

"It's now much more openly spoken about, realising that quite young children can be depressed, for instance.

" Certainly for me, I didn't know anyone else who was depressed when I was a child. "

* Judith's last name has been withheld by request

World.title: $4.3m pilot to help victim-survivors navigate NSW justice system
World.content:
Specialist workers will be deployed across New South Wales to help victim-survivors of sexual assault navigate the justice system under a trial welcomed by one support service as "a big step forward".

Eleven justice system navigators will be employed under the $4.3 million, two-year pilot to offer victim-survivors older than 16 guidance and information on police and court processes and connect them with other supports.

Tenders have been awarded to services across the state, including Full Stop Australia, which has received funding to employ one specialist worker to service metropolitan Sydney.

Karen Bevan says her organisation has spent a number of years lobbying for the pilot program. (ABC News: Abby Haberecht)

Full Stop Australia chief executive Karen Bevan said the organisation had been lobbying for a justice system navigator program since 2022 and hoped to recruit a worker "quite soon".

"We've been arguing specifically for this kind of program in one version or another since 2022, so it's really important for us that we are part of it but also that the program even exists is a big step forward," Ms Bevan said.

"I'm really hoping that this will be a part of a process that puts victim-survivors at the centre and supports them as they make choices that are right for them.

" We really hope that it becomes not just a once-off referral, but someone who walks through this process with you, which is something that victim-survivors have said over and over that they need. "

Victim-survivors will not have to make a police complaint to access the support.

Rather, the navigators will help people understand their options, the justice system processes and how to access other supports.

"We really hope that this program delivers an ongoing, consistent set of supports through the process of what happens after a sexual assault," Ms Bevan said.

"We hope it supports people who want to make reports to police, who are going through investigations and court systems, and we hope it supports people who are looking to identify services that will help them with the trauma and experience that they've had."

Complainants in sexual assault cases have previously told the ABC of the negative impacts of feeling uninformed and confused about police and court processes.

The NSW pilot has been funded by the state and federal governments.

A version of the program will operate in every state and territory.

'One of the hardest things a person will ever do'

Federal Assistant Minister for Social Services and the Prevention of Family Violence Ged Kearney said reporting sexual violence was "one of the hardest things a person will ever do", with justice system navigators aimed at helping make the process easier.

"Many victim-survivors tell us they feel frightened, confused and overwhelmed after reporting sexual violence," Ms Kearney said.

" The sexual violence justice system navigators provide practical support and continuity of trauma-informed care so women don't have to face the journey alone. "

NSW Minister for the Prevention of Domestic Violence and Sexual Assault Jodie Harrison agreed: "By investing in community-based justice system navigators, it’s easier for victim-survivors to access support throughout the criminal justice process while linking them with community organisations, legal services and government agencies."

A similar program has operated in England and Wales since 2007.

A 2020 survey by the Victims' Commissioner for England and Wales found victim-survivors who received assistance from an independent sexual violence advisor or other support service were significantly less likely to stop supporting an investigation or prosecution.

World.title: Hospital faces 'day of reckoning' as CEO departs and ED overwhelmed
World.content:
A major Victorian hospital is looking to restructure after the mysterious departure of its chief executive while its emergency department struggles with a reduction in locum and agency staff.

The Mildura Base Public Hospital (MBPH), one of the largest employers in north-west Victoria, has been under the control of an acting chief executive since Terry Welch left the organisation without notice one month ago.

The hospital is yet to confirm the reason for Mr Welch's departure.

The ABC can reveal one of MBPH's seven executive directors, Heath Kendall, accepted a redundancy package from the hospital last week.

Mr Kendall oversaw the hospital's corporate and community affairs, as well as the MBPH Foundation, a fundraising body.

Heath Kendall's profile was removed from the MBPH website this week. (Supplied: MBPH)

The move comes ahead of a proposed restructure to reduce the number of executives from seven to five, which the hospital said would strengthen accountability and improve decision-making.

However a number of staff, past and present, have voiced frustrations about MBPH's handling of Mr Welch's departure and its expenditure on non-clinical positions, which staff said had contributed to budgetary pressure.

A nurse who spoke on the condition of anonymity said Mr Welch's departure coincided with a noted reduction in the number of locum doctors and agency nurses available in the emergency department.

They said nurses were working double shifts as a result, resulting in more staff calling in sick due to burnout.

"Honestly, I think that the bottom line is that it will be affecting patient care," the ED nurse said.

" Staff in ED have been exhausted and sort of feeling pushed to their absolute limit for quite some time now. "

An internal memo about staffing from earlier this month said new recruiting arrangements were designed to keep the hospital "financially sustainable".

The memo, seen by the ABC, said reliance on agency and locum staff had been "higher than planned and considerably above historical levels".

According to the hospital's latest annual report, MBPH has more than $41 million in payable liabilities, a figure that almost doubled from the previous financial year.

Do you know more? Contact Daniel Miles using danielgmiles@protonmail.com

If you require more secure communication, please choose an option on the confidential tips page

MBPH has categorically denied suggestions of a hiring freeze, but would not comment specifically about changes to the number of agency or locum staff employed.

A senior medical professional from the region, also speaking on the condition on anonymity, said the hospital was facing "a day of reckoning".

"Since the hospital's change back to public management, a lot of non-clinical staff have been employed, causing budget blowouts with no consequential improvements for patient outcomes," they said.

" It's a day of reckoning. You can't put on a whole heap of non-clinical staff when the focus should really be on patient outcomes and access to care. "

Mildura Base Public Hospital services about 80,000 people in the state's north-west. (ABC Mildura-Swan Hill: Wade Stephens)

Frustration remains

MBPH services the Sunraysia region, which has a population of almost 80,000.

It is among the regional Victorian hospitals struggling to cope with emergency department numbers, with some patients often spending longer than 24 hours in ED.

Acting chief executive Matthew Jukes would not be drawn on the reason for his Mr Welch's exit, which he said was a matter for the hospital board and Victorian health department.

"The challenge we obviously have is the consultation processes sometimes need to remain confidential as part of the employment matters," Mr Jukes said.

"And, unfortunately, sometimes it's just not appropriate for us to comment on individual employees."

Terry Welch maintained a presence in local media and at fundraising events. (Supplied: Mildura Base Public Hospital)

A government spokesperson said Mr Welch's departure was a matter for MBPH and its board.

Mr Jukes said the proposed changes to the executive would not affect the hospital's ability to serve the community.

"No changes are being made to the patient services that are provided as part of what we're doing," he said.

"Financial sustainability is one consideration, but it's not the sole purpose of the proposal.

"No final decision has been made, as we're working through the consultation process with the affected employees and the relevant unions."

Matthew Jukes declined to comment on whether budgetary constraints were affecting staff numbers. (Supplied: Mildura Base Public Hospital)

Mr Jukes said the hospital had introduced "oversights and some controls" regarding recruitment as part of a focus on a sustainable, local workforce.

He would not comment on whether fewer locum or agency staff were being employed due to budgetary constraints.

"We have made really important progress towards reducing our reliance on high-cost workforce, which is typically your fly-in agency and locums," Mr Jukes said.

"We still recognise that they are an absolutely integral part of us being able to deliver service, and we'll have to continue and will continue to engage in external workforce to be able to deliver our service.

"But absolutely our priority is to build a workforce that is sustainable and local."

Liberal MP Georgie Crozier raised MBPH's staffing issues during Question Time in state parliament last Wednesday, stating she had been informed the hospital would be without locum staff for six months due to budget constraints.

A Victorian Health Department spokesperson said MBPH was strengthening the "oversight of workforce and recruitment decisions" to ensure spending is responsible.

"There is not a freeze on locum doctors or recruitment at Mildura Base Public Hospital, and there is no impact on patient care of the hospital's ability to deliver services," the spokesperson said.

The Victorian branches of the Australian Nursing and Midwifery Federation and Health Services Union have been contacted for comment.

The MBPH board has also been contacted for comment.

World.title: ‘You can imagine what it smells like’: The monster your wet wipes create
World.content:
NationalQueenslandCity council ‘You can imagine what it smells like’: The monster your wet wipes create Julius Dennis August 19, 2026 — 6:55am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Plenty of weird things are pulled out of Brisbane’s sewerage system – toys, phones, false teeth, half a surfboard and even a snake – but if you ask the man responsible for looking after those pipes, they’ve got nothing on wet wipes. The wipes, flushed from toilets around the city, become glued together by a mash of sewage to form long, dark monsters known as fatbergs. “You can imagine what it smells like,” said David Brooker, Urban Utilities’ executive leader of operations and maintenance. Loading Brooker runs a team of hundreds: a 24/7 on-call team to deal with blockages, a monitoring centre at the company’s Fortitude Valley headquarters, engineers and support staff, and a legion of workers chipping away at upgrading the network.



Urban Utilities look after more than 20,000 kilometres of pipe (half water, half wastewater), 28 wastewater treatment plants and 348 wastewater pump stations across Brisbane, Ipswich, the Scenic Rim, Somerset and Lockyer Valley councils. Despite the size of the team, Brooker said they can’t know what’s happening throughout the whole system at all times. David Brooker in front of the control room monitoring more than 20,000 kilometres of pipe. Julius Dennis “Because all this infrastructure is buried, you can’t actually see every bit of the infrastructure all the time,” he said. In 2025, the 3000 blockages in the wastewater cost nearly $3 million to fix, according to the company.



“What we’re really wanting people to be aware of is what they put down their toilet and sink really matters,” Brooker said. What can seem like a harmless splash of oil or fat down the drain after frying up a meal can lead to big problems for the network. Then there’s the wet wipes. “We certainly are seeing an increase in wet wipe use, so we see them turning up at our treatment plants much, much more now than we did five and certainly 10 years ago.” Wet wipes pulled from the network at the Luggage Point water treatment plant. Urban Utilities



These wipes, even some labelled as flushable, don’t break down like conventional toilet paper, and when they meet with the oils and fats coming from kitchens around the city they can create a monster. “It can clump up in pipes, it clogs up pumps or clogs up our treatment plants,” Brooker said. A record-breaking 500 kilogram fatberg found in 2021. Urban Utilities Fatbergs, responsible for about 20 per cent of the network’s blockages, had a national moment last year when they were blamed for mysterious round objects – eventually named “poo balls” – washing up on Sydney beaches. Brooker said that won’t happen in Brisbane as the water is treated heavily before it makes its way to Moreton Bay, but that doesn’t mean they’re good for the system or enjoyable to work with.



“It’s wastewater or sewage that might have been stuck there for a few days or up to a few weeks if it gets clumped – it’s not a pleasant experience.” Avoiding wipes that don’t break down and wiping oils from pans and popping that the bin would go a long way, Brooker said. However, tree roots chasing water are the greatest challenge, with Urban Utilities deploying a routine program to find susceptible areas of the up to 100-year-old network to look out for thirsty plants. The company’s awareness push around what can go down the drain – which includes a comic titled Rise of the Fatberg handed out at the Ekka – coincides with increased media attention in the Brisbane network, which saw a series of memorable bursts last year, and the company having to walk back planned increases to bulk water charges. Loading



“A few people have done some reports saying: ‘Hey, we’re getting to a stage in our network where we’ve got to start to manage [it] a little bit differently because if we don’t, things come to the end of their useful life,’” Brooker said. He said network upgrades, both through the cheap option of re-lining old pipes and the expensive one of duplicating them, have much more to do with population growth than the age of the system. “The price of your water bill is really heavily dominated by the cost of that infrastructure that’s in the ground, so the way we can efficiently serve and keep the prices down in the long run is by really making sure these assets are being used well and as long to their full capacity as possible. World.title: Australia news LIVE: Gambling reform package passes House of Representatives; Sweeping NDIS cuts expected to become law this week
World.content:
Federal and state governments must urgently start work on setting up new disability systems for older children, teenagers and adults with lower needs after the parliament this week passes laws that will remove 240,000 people from the National Disability Insurance Scheme.

Health and Disability Minister Mark Butler said a scheme akin to a “Thriving Teens” program would need to get off the ground within the next 16 months to make sure older children who no longer qualified for the scheme aren’t left in the lurch when eligibility changes start in 2028.

Labor sealed an agreement with the Coalition yesterday to pass its contentious NDIS overhaul, which should recoup $37 billion for the federal budget in the next four years, and $150 billion in a decade. The bill passed the Senate with a tranche of amendments on Tuesday night, and will return to the House this week to become law.

Minister for Health Mark Butler during a press conference in Canberra yesterday. Dominic Lorrimer

Butler said federal officials were already designing new NDIS eligibility assessments that will come into effect in January 2028, but there was plenty of work to be done by then so that new systems will be ready to cater to people who no longer qualified for the $50 billion scheme under stricter criteria.

State governments, except for Queensland, have implementation plans ready and to start rolling out the Thriving Kids scheme for children under nine with development delays and autism from October this year, with its complete rollout due by the start of 2028.

World.title: ASX set to dip, Wall Street slumps as AI stocks fall
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to dip, Wall Street slumps as AI stocks fall Stan Choe Updated August 19, 2026 — 6:27am ,first published 5:19am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Wall Street pulled further from its all-time high as AI stocks got back to sinking. The S&P 500 fell 0.7 per cent for a third straight modest loss since setting its all-time high on Thursday. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dipped 116 points, or 0.2 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite sank 1.3 per cent. AI stocks have been volatile in the northern hemisphere summer. Bloomberg The Australian sharemarket is set to dip, with futures at 4.54am AEST pointing to a dip of 6 points, or 0.1 per cent, at the open. The ASX closed flat on Tuesday. The Australian dollar is weaker at US70.83¢. It’s another busy day on the reporting season calendar with Santos and Yancoal among companies due up. Leading the way lower were stocks that have been big winners in the boom around artificial-intelligence technology. They’ve been veering up and down this summer on worries that their prices shot too high in the AI frenzy and that the strong demand for memory, processors and other building blocks of data centers may fizzle out if AI proves less profitable than promised.



Related Article Opinion

World markets Red alert: This chart says Wall Street is ready to crash Micron Technology dropped 7 per cent, and the seller of computer memory was one of the heaviest weights on the S&P 500. So were chip companies Nvidia, which fell 2.3 per cent, and Broadcom, which sank 3.2 per cent. Even with their recent swings, such stocks remain big winners, and Micron has more than tripled this year. But stocks that critics call too expensive get more scrutiny when interest rates are high, and yields remained that way in bond markets worldwide on Tuesday. The yield on the 10-year US Treasury edged down to 4.70 per cent from 4.72 per cent late Monday but remains well above its 3.97 per cent level from just before the war with Iran began. The 30-year Treasury yield also ticked lower but is still near its highest level since 2007.



Yields have jumped since the war began because high oil prices are pushing upward on inflation. All the while, continuing worries about huge debt loads for governments and their increases in borrowing keep yields high. When yields are high, investors are less willing to pay high prices for stocks and other kinds of investments, particularly those seen as the most expensive. Much of the pressure on yields has come from oil prices, and Brent crude added 0.2 per cent to $91.02 per barrel. It’s been swinging sharply on uncertainty about when and whether the United States and Iran can reach a deal to allow oil tankers to exit the Persian Gulf freely again. Brent was going for $72.87 per barrel just before the start of the war. High yields have already sent the average long-term US mortgage rate near its highest level in a year, which has hurt the housing industry. A report on Tuesday said homebuilders broke ground on fewer new houses last month than economists expected. Such data helped to restrain Home Depot’s stock, which slipped 0.1 per cent even though the retailer reported stronger profit and revenue for the latest quarter than analysts expected. Chief Financial Officer Richard McPhail said Home Depot saw its customers continue to pursue smaller projects.



High yields could also slow the borrowing Big Tech companies are doing to pay for data centres, putting at risk one of the big sources of growth for the US economy. Related Article Opinion

Biotech Changing fortunes: Is biotech giant CSL’s $10b write-down a comeback story? Elizabeth Knight Business columnist Elsewhere on Wall Street, Klarna fell 22.8 per cent even though the payments company reported stronger results for the latest quarter than analysts expected. The buy-now, pay-later company cut some of its financial forecasts for 2026, largely because of expectations for Germany, its largest market by volume. Meta Platforms fell 4.4 per cent as opening statements began in a pivotal trial in a California federal court, where states are seeking billions of dollars in damages for social media harms to children. All told, the S&P 500 fell 53.30 points to 7,691.76. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dipped 116.38 to 53,343.40, and the Nasdaq composite sank 355.20 to 26,289.71.



In stock markets abroad, indexes were mixed in Europe and Asia. South Korea’s Kospi fell 1.5 per cent, which counts as relatively modest move for it. It had swung by at least 2.4 per cent in each of its three prior days. Seoul’s market has been home to some of the world’s sharpest AI-induced swings because it’s dominated by two tech giants, Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix. World.title: ‘Don’t call it a rebel league’: Inside surfing’s new $20m Big Bash-style comp
World.content:
SportSurfing ‘Don’t call it a rebel league’: Inside surfing’s new $20m Big Bash-style comp Dan Walsh August 19, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

An ambitious “made for TV” summer surfing league will launch with the promise of career-changing $10,000 weekly wages for Australian surfers on the basis of team franchises being sold to cover the competition’s estimated $20 million running costs. The Surfing Super League (SSL), a nine-week “home-and-away” season to be contested by eight teams along the east coast of Australia from January 2028, has been unveiled by majority owner and former Surfing Australia chief executive Chris Mater. Owen Wright (left) will come out of competitive retirement to compete in the Surfing Super League, a new venture led by CEO and founder Chris Mater. Sam Mooy The breakaway league is pitching as an alternative to traditional one-on-one professional surfing formats, which feature multi-week, condition-based competition windows at world-class waves. Instead, the SSL will feature teams of four surfers contesting a 90-minute, relay-based event in fixed Saturday and Sunday afternoon timeslots across school holidays.



The league aims to offer guaranteed broadcast content regardless of conditions in what are traditionally less reliable summer months for quality waves and swell, at spectator-friendly beach venues. Surfing Australia, the sport’s governing body domestically, is not involved in the start-up league. Surfing Australia representatives could not be reached for comment. Olympic bronze medallist Owen Wright, big-wave record-holder Laura Enever and former world No.2 Bede Durbidge have signed on as the competition’s biggest names, which will target “out-of-market” domestic and international surfers, along with Australia’s next generation rather than established surfers already competing on the WSL’s Championship Tour. Documents registered with the Australian Securities and Investments Commission show the SSL was initially valued at approximately $13.53 million based on the $483,333 seed investment for a 3.6 per cent stake by David Elsworth, an Australian entrepreneur whose background includes high-level marketing roles with Coca-Cola in Japan and ownership of a Japanese gin distillery and pet care company.



The league’s valuation has since been marked as significantly higher. Mater is confident of locking in a broadcast partner as negotiations with DAZN, owners of subscription platform Kayo, continue, while free-to-air providers Nine, Seven and Ten have also been approached. Mater will now begin a market search for a principal partner and sponsors for each of the eight franchises. In total, Mater predicts running the start-up league will cost “north of $20 million in season one”, with $89,000 wages for 48 surfers (each franchise will have a squad of six, four men and two women) amounting to more than $4.2 million in salaries alone. Marketed as “the Big Bash of surfing” with a nod to cricket’s T20 format and franchise-based competitions, SSL’s business modelling projects for two of the eight teams to be sold to private investors in order to turn a profit after its first season.



“I wouldn’t call this a rebel league at all,” Mater told this masthead. “I think it’s a complementary league [to the WSL’s world tour]. Or I would ask, is the V8 Supercars a rebel league? This is a format Australian surfing needs. We’re not trying to compete with the WSL. “There’s a big gap in the domestic market given pro surfing focuses on the international stage, and the national bodies focus on junior development. “But what we’re doing is creating a real ‘made for TV’ event, and a pathway for Australian surfers to compete in a very different format that opens surfing up in a new way to broadcasters and fans”. The SSL’s January-February season would land in the WSL’s off-season as well as a window between cricket’s Test schedule and the NRL and AFL seasons. “It’s going to change lives for the next generation”: Owen Wright. Sam Mooy



The new venture’s format and schedule will, however, potentially collide with Surfing Australia’s own teams-based Boardrider Battle, which runs across seven east coast events before a grand final in March. By locking events into specific summer timeslots, though, SSL organisers risk surfers regularly competing in blown-out, poor quality waves. “And if you’re in a traditional one-on-one surfing heat, you cannot run an event in poor surf,” Mater said. “There’s too much of surfers waiting around, it’s just deadset boring. The teams format adds an ironman element where you’re racing the clock with 40 minutes to get your surfers in and out of the water, catching as many waves as they need to win the game. Former WCT surfer Sophie McCulloch has signed on with the Surfing Super League. Andrew Shield



“It’s a really dynamic format that allows us to run in less than ideal conditions.” The proposed $89,000 contracts for all SSL surfers, regardless of gender or competition status, are a significant selling point given the gulf between surfing’s elite and athletes on the world tour’s fringe and below. Super Surf League founder and majority share-holder Chris Mater. Sam Mooy Surfers like reigning world champion Molly Picklum and leading Australian men Jack Robinson and Ethan Ewing hold non-compete clauses in their WSL contracts, which require express permission for them to compete in other events, and as a result, are not being targeted by SSL. “The kind of money we’re talking about for more than a handful of Australian surfers here is unheard of,” Wright said.



“It’s going to change lives for the next generation. It can help someone pursue a professional career, and take a real run at the WCT with all the travel and costs that involves. The market around things like individual sponsors is really shifting, so that’s a big reason why I’m so passionate about this format”. Mater resigned as Surfing Australia chief executive in late-2025 after seven years in charge and describes the sport as “one of the country’s most powerful untapped commercial opportunities”. He believes grassroots investment and under 18s and under 21s competitions around each regional franchise will help create genuine fan engagement and in turn, attract private investors. “We’ll run the league in the first season and our model is budgeting for at the end of that first season, we’ll have proven it’s successful with crowds, TV ratings and our events,” Mater said. “We’ll then be selling two of the eight teams. And each season we’re going to sell another two, plan to introduce two more franchises by season five and create a big engine of revenue and profit on top of a model that already takes in sponsors, ticketing, merchandise and a diversified revenue stream.” News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday.

World.title: Princess Diana’s brother writes new book about her, vowing to correct ‘untruths’
World.content:
WorldEuropePrincess Diana Princess Diana’s brother writes new book about her, vowing to correct ‘untruths’ India McTaggart August 19, 2026 — 5:57am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

London: Earl Spencer will publish a book about his sister Diana, Princess of Wales, to correct “untruths that have become accepted” about the late princess. The memoir, titled Swan Song: Diana, My Sister, is set to be released next month to mark the 30th anniversary of her death next year. Diana, Princess of Wales, wearing the Lover’s Knot Tiara on a 1985 visit to Washington. Getty It is expected to cover the princess’s childhood; her unhappy marriage to Charles, the then Prince of Wales; and the aftermath of her death in a car crash in Paris on August 31, 1997. Lord Spencer, Diana’s younger brother, said the aim of the book was “to tell the truth about Diana from her brother’s perspective, just as I attempted to do when speaking at her funeral”.



In September 1997, Lord Spencer delivered a eulogy at the funeral of his sister in Westminster Abbey that was later named one of the greatest speeches of the 20th century. He has described the new book as a continuation of his tribute nearly 30 years ago, explaining: “As with my eulogy, I want to speak on Diana’s behalf and do so in an openly positive way. Earl Spencer with Diana’s son, Prince Harry, in 2021. AP “I hope this book will be of interest to the many who still cherish the memory of Diana when she was alive,” he said. “And I would be delighted if those too young to remember her in her heyday feel – after reading this – that they ‘get’ who she really was: a one-off, dynamic character, full of love, charisma and self-doubt, who gave life a hell of a go, and left the world a far better place, despite exiting the stage while still so young.”



Lord Spencer said he decided to write a memoir about his sister after being “inundated” with requests for interviews to mark the three decades since her death. “This has convinced me to write down my own thoughts and memories, once and for all, rather than having the discomfort of again reading the opinions of others, many of which are based on untruths that have become accepted over time,” he said. Charles and Diana at Sydney Opera House in 1983. Getty Images The book, which will be published around the world and translated into 12 languages, is also expected to provide an insider’s account of how the royal family dealt with the public’s grief and anger following the princess’s death. In his own memoir, the Duke of Sussex claimed that there was a heated behind-the-scenes debate about whether he and the then-Prince William should walk behind his mother’s coffin at her funeral.



The Duke revealed in his book Spare that Lord Spencer objected vocally to the idea of the two young princes following the funeral cortège, describing it as “a barbarity” at the time. However, he said that when an alternative plan was suggested of having Prince William, then aged 15, walk alone behind the coffin the Duke objected – saying he did not want his brother to undergo the ordeal on his own. William (left) and Harry at their mother’s funeral in 1997. AP The Duke claimed that his uncle “flew into a rage” about the difficult decision, saying: “You cannot force these children to walk behind their mother’s coffin. It’s a barbarity!” Last year, Lord Spencer said he found it “difficult” when strangers recounted where they were when his sister died.



He made the comments while discussing how he becomes “fundamentally unhappy” on the anniversary of the princess’s death. Speaking to Gyles Brandreth on the author’s podcast, Rosebud, he said: “I tell you what I do find quite difficult … it probably sounds ungracious but occasionally total strangers come up and feel they must tell me where they were when they heard she died. The car from the crash that killed Diana and Dodi Fayed in 1997. AP “I’m sure that’s helpful to them, it’s not entirely helpful to everyone else.” He went on to give an example of an American woman, whom he said, “clutched me to her ample bosom and said that I may have thought I grew up with Diana, but actually, she did in South Dakota”.



Lord Spencer added: “You just have to smile, it doesn’t matter”. His new book is set to be published in the UK by Penguin Michael Joseph, a division of Penguin Random House, on September 22. Diana with Queen Elizabeth II in 1987. AP Swan Song features a black-and-white photograph of Diana on its cover. Daniel Bunyard, the publisher who acquired the global rights for the book, said: “This is a book of historic importance, telling as it does the story of one of the 20th century’s most iconic and culturally significant figures, but it is also unique in being written by Earl Spencer, from a vantage point of such intimacy.



Related Article Royal family Prince of Wales shares unseen Diana photograph for Mother’s Day “Charles Spencer is a loving brother and an acclaimed memoirist as well as a celebrated historian, and all these facets are brought together in Swan Song. “It is moving, beautifully written and remarkably candid, in no small part due to Charles’s ability to access great emotional depth without sentimentality, honest observation without rancour, and warmth without gloss. “Readers will find for the first time, but also for all time, a fitting tribute to Princess Diana.” Telegraph, London Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: ‘Meta needed kids’: Tech giant on trial over social media addiction
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaSocial media ‘Meta needed kids’: Tech giant on trial over social media addiction Diana Novak Jones and Jonathan Stempel Updated August 19, 2026 — 5:37am ,first published 3:20am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Meta Platforms intentionally sought to addict children to its Facebook and Instagram platforms in pursuit of profit, a lawyer for California said on Tuesday (US time) at the start of a trial that could reshape some of the most popular apps on the planet. A bipartisan group of 29 US states is suing Meta, seeking potentially tens or hundreds of billions of dollars in penalties and changes to how Meta does business. Loading Four lead states – California, Colorado, Kentucky and New Jersey – accuse Meta of designing Facebook and Instagram to hook young users, fuelling anxiety, depression and even suicide, and misleading consumers about the platforms’ safety. Jurors will hear claims by all 29 states that Meta violated federal law by improperly collecting and using personal data of children while they used its platforms.



Megan O’Neill, a deputy attorney general for California, told an eight-person jury in her opening statement that Meta’s business model was to “hook the users, hold them for as long as they can, harvest their data, and then hide the truth from the public.” “It worked especially well for kids,” O’Neill added. “Meta needed kids, and it needed to reassure the people who cared about those kids that the kids are safe.” The Ronald V. Dellums Federal Building and US Courthouse in Oakland, California. Bloomberg Meta’s lawyer Paul Schmidt countered in his opening statement that the company and its co-founder and chief executive Mark Zuckerberg shared a desire to improve their services, not to make them dangerous. “They don’t believe they’re going to do well if people don’t like their service,” Schmidt said.



Jurors in the Oakland, California, federal court are expected to issue an advisory verdict, but US District Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers will determine Meta’s liability. Related Article Social media Meta and Google found liable in landmark social media addiction trial If she finds Meta liable, Rogers could impose civil penalties and order changes to Facebook and Instagram. Meta has said it did not make misleading statements about safety, and the states failed to show their residents were harmed. Zuckerberg and Instagram chief Adam Mosseri are expected to testify. The trial is scheduled to last six weeks.



Experts have said the trial is the biggest legal test yet of social media’s effects on young users, and comes amid a broader reckoning across the globe over those effects. Meta has said penalties could be as high as $US1.4 trillion ($1.97 trillion), close to the Menlo Park, California-based company’s market value. California Attorney General Rob Bonta arrives at the courthouse on Tuesday. AP Photo/Noah Berger Attorneys general have yet to specify penalties but said at a hearing last week the amount could be closer to $US200 billion ($282 billion) – equivalent to about three years of after-tax profit for Meta. California, Colorado, Kentucky and New Jersey also want Meta to implement age restrictions, and eliminate the infinite scroll that encourages users to keep looking at new posts.



O’Neill said the states were not trying to put Meta, or social media, out of business. “This case is not about whether social media has some benefits for some people. It does,” she said. Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, pictured in February, is expected to give evidence. Bloomberg But she said Meta exploited children for its own benefit, researching how children’s brains work and would react to online stimuli, and tracking every interaction that children had on its apps. She showed jurors an internal email sent to Mosseri, which said “teen time spent” was the company’s goal, and said Meta employees viewed Instagram as a “drug” and themselves as “pushers”.



“Meta found the younger a kid is when they start using the app, the better,” O’Neill said. “The more likely they are to remain a user, the more likely they are to make Meta money in the long run.” Related Article Online gambling Facebook is advertising illegal gambling, and the watchdog is powerless to stop it Schmidt acknowledged that employees might use “loose” language in private, but jurors would hear what the employee who called Instagram a drug then did to make it safer. Some critics of Meta spoke outside the courthouse as the trial began. Among them was Mary Rodee, who said her 15-year-old son Riley Basford was victimised by a predator on Facebook before he died by suicide in 2021.



“They call it spontaneous suicide,” she said. “I call it what it was, the predictable outcome of a system that protects corporations instead of children.” The lawsuit began in 2023, two years after whistleblower Frances Haugen testified to a US Senate committee that Meta knew its products were unsafe for children and knew how to fix the problem, but did nothing in favour of pursuing higher profits. Meta and other social media companies including Snap, TikTok parent ByteDance and YouTube parent Alphabet face thousands of lawsuits by states, municipalities, school districts and individuals over whether their products harm young users. In March, a Los Angeles jury ordered Meta and Google to pay $US6 million to a 20-year-old woman who said she became addicted to Instagram and YouTube media as a child. Earlier this month, a New Mexico judge ordered Meta to pay $US567 million into a mental health fund for teenagers after that state’s attorney general said the company’s platforms were a public nuisance.

World.title: ‘You can imagine what it smells like’: The monster your wet wipes create
World.content:
NationalQueenslandCity council ‘You can imagine what it smells like’: The monster your wet wipes create Julius Dennis August 19, 2026 — 6:55am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Plenty of weird things are pulled out of Brisbane’s sewerage system – toys, phones, false teeth, half a surfboard and even a snake – but if you ask the man responsible for looking after those pipes, they’ve got nothing on wet wipes. The wipes, flushed from toilets around the city, become glued together by a mash of sewage to form long, dark monsters known as fatbergs. “You can imagine what it smells like,” said David Brooker, Urban Utilities’ executive leader of operations and maintenance. Loading Brooker runs a team of hundreds: a 24/7 on-call team to deal with blockages, a monitoring centre at the company’s Fortitude Valley headquarters, engineers and support staff, and a legion of workers chipping away at upgrading the network.



Urban Utilities look after more than 20,000 kilometres of pipe (half water, half wastewater), 28 wastewater treatment plants and 348 wastewater pump stations across Brisbane, Ipswich, the Scenic Rim, Somerset and Lockyer Valley councils. Despite the size of the team, Brooker said they can’t know what’s happening throughout the whole system at all times. David Brooker in front of the control room monitoring more than 20,000 kilometres of pipe. Julius Dennis “Because all this infrastructure is buried, you can’t actually see every bit of the infrastructure all the time,” he said. In 2025, the 3000 blockages in the wastewater cost nearly $3 million to fix, according to the company.



“What we’re really wanting people to be aware of is what they put down their toilet and sink really matters,” Brooker said. What can seem like a harmless splash of oil or fat down the drain after frying up a meal can lead to big problems for the network. Then there’s the wet wipes. “We certainly are seeing an increase in wet wipe use, so we see them turning up at our treatment plants much, much more now than we did five and certainly 10 years ago.” Wet wipes pulled from the network at the Luggage Point water treatment plant. Urban Utilities



These wipes, even some labelled as flushable, don’t break down like conventional toilet paper, and when they meet with the oils and fats coming from kitchens around the city they can create a monster. “It can clump up in pipes, it clogs up pumps or clogs up our treatment plants,” Brooker said. A record-breaking 500 kilogram fatberg found in 2021. Urban Utilities Fatbergs, responsible for about 20 per cent of the network’s blockages, had a national moment last year when they were blamed for mysterious round objects – eventually named “poo balls” – washing up on Sydney beaches. Brooker said that won’t happen in Brisbane as the water is treated heavily before it makes its way to Moreton Bay, but that doesn’t mean they’re good for the system or enjoyable to work with.



“It’s wastewater or sewage that might have been stuck there for a few days or up to a few weeks if it gets clumped – it’s not a pleasant experience.” Avoiding wipes that don’t break down and wiping oils from pans and popping that the bin would go a long way, Brooker said. However, tree roots chasing water are the greatest challenge, with Urban Utilities deploying a routine program to find susceptible areas of the up to 100-year-old network to look out for thirsty plants. The company’s awareness push around what can go down the drain – which includes a comic titled Rise of the Fatberg handed out at the Ekka – coincides with increased media attention in the Brisbane network, which saw a series of memorable bursts last year, and the company having to walk back planned increases to bulk water charges. Loading



“A few people have done some reports saying: ‘Hey, we’re getting to a stage in our network where we’ve got to start to manage [it] a little bit differently because if we don’t, things come to the end of their useful life,’” Brooker said. He said network upgrades, both through the cheap option of re-lining old pipes and the expensive one of duplicating them, have much more to do with population growth than the age of the system. “The price of your water bill is really heavily dominated by the cost of that infrastructure that’s in the ground, so the way we can efficiently serve and keep the prices down in the long run is by really making sure these assets are being used well and as long to their full capacity as possible. World.title: Australia news LIVE: Gambling reform package passes House of Representatives; Sweeping NDIS cuts expected to become law this week
World.content:
Federal and state governments must urgently start work on setting up new disability systems for older children, teenagers and adults with lower needs after the parliament this week passes laws that will remove 240,000 people from the National Disability Insurance Scheme.

Health and Disability Minister Mark Butler said a scheme akin to a “Thriving Teens” program would need to get off the ground within the next 16 months to make sure older children who no longer qualified for the scheme aren’t left in the lurch when eligibility changes start in 2028.

Labor sealed an agreement with the Coalition yesterday to pass its contentious NDIS overhaul, which should recoup $37 billion for the federal budget in the next four years, and $150 billion in a decade. The bill passed the Senate with a tranche of amendments on Tuesday night, and will return to the House this week to become law.

Minister for Health Mark Butler during a press conference in Canberra yesterday. Dominic Lorrimer

Butler said federal officials were already designing new NDIS eligibility assessments that will come into effect in January 2028, but there was plenty of work to be done by then so that new systems will be ready to cater to people who no longer qualified for the $50 billion scheme under stricter criteria.

State governments, except for Queensland, have implementation plans ready and to start rolling out the Thriving Kids scheme for children under nine with development delays and autism from October this year, with its complete rollout due by the start of 2028.

World.title: ASX set to dip, Wall Street slumps as AI stocks fall
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to dip, Wall Street slumps as AI stocks fall Stan Choe Updated August 19, 2026 — 6:27am ,first published 5:19am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Wall Street pulled further from its all-time high as AI stocks got back to sinking. The S&P 500 fell 0.7 per cent for a third straight modest loss since setting its all-time high on Thursday. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dipped 116 points, or 0.2 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite sank 1.3 per cent. AI stocks have been volatile in the northern hemisphere summer. Bloomberg The Australian sharemarket is set to dip, with futures at 4.54am AEST pointing to a dip of 6 points, or 0.1 per cent, at the open. The ASX closed flat on Tuesday. The Australian dollar is weaker at US70.83¢. It’s another busy day on the reporting season calendar with Santos and Yancoal among companies due up. Leading the way lower were stocks that have been big winners in the boom around artificial-intelligence technology. They’ve been veering up and down this summer on worries that their prices shot too high in the AI frenzy and that the strong demand for memory, processors and other building blocks of data centers may fizzle out if AI proves less profitable than promised.



Related Article Opinion

World markets Red alert: This chart says Wall Street is ready to crash Micron Technology dropped 7 per cent, and the seller of computer memory was one of the heaviest weights on the S&P 500. So were chip companies Nvidia, which fell 2.3 per cent, and Broadcom, which sank 3.2 per cent. Even with their recent swings, such stocks remain big winners, and Micron has more than tripled this year. But stocks that critics call too expensive get more scrutiny when interest rates are high, and yields remained that way in bond markets worldwide on Tuesday. The yield on the 10-year US Treasury edged down to 4.70 per cent from 4.72 per cent late Monday but remains well above its 3.97 per cent level from just before the war with Iran began. The 30-year Treasury yield also ticked lower but is still near its highest level since 2007.



Yields have jumped since the war began because high oil prices are pushing upward on inflation. All the while, continuing worries about huge debt loads for governments and their increases in borrowing keep yields high. When yields are high, investors are less willing to pay high prices for stocks and other kinds of investments, particularly those seen as the most expensive. Much of the pressure on yields has come from oil prices, and Brent crude added 0.2 per cent to $91.02 per barrel. It’s been swinging sharply on uncertainty about when and whether the United States and Iran can reach a deal to allow oil tankers to exit the Persian Gulf freely again. Brent was going for $72.87 per barrel just before the start of the war. High yields have already sent the average long-term US mortgage rate near its highest level in a year, which has hurt the housing industry. A report on Tuesday said homebuilders broke ground on fewer new houses last month than economists expected. Such data helped to restrain Home Depot’s stock, which slipped 0.1 per cent even though the retailer reported stronger profit and revenue for the latest quarter than analysts expected. Chief Financial Officer Richard McPhail said Home Depot saw its customers continue to pursue smaller projects.



High yields could also slow the borrowing Big Tech companies are doing to pay for data centres, putting at risk one of the big sources of growth for the US economy. Related Article Opinion

Biotech Changing fortunes: Is biotech giant CSL’s $10b write-down a comeback story? Elizabeth Knight Business columnist Elsewhere on Wall Street, Klarna fell 22.8 per cent even though the payments company reported stronger results for the latest quarter than analysts expected. The buy-now, pay-later company cut some of its financial forecasts for 2026, largely because of expectations for Germany, its largest market by volume. Meta Platforms fell 4.4 per cent as opening statements began in a pivotal trial in a California federal court, where states are seeking billions of dollars in damages for social media harms to children. All told, the S&P 500 fell 53.30 points to 7,691.76. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dipped 116.38 to 53,343.40, and the Nasdaq composite sank 355.20 to 26,289.71.



In stock markets abroad, indexes were mixed in Europe and Asia. South Korea’s Kospi fell 1.5 per cent, which counts as relatively modest move for it. It had swung by at least 2.4 per cent in each of its three prior days. Seoul’s market has been home to some of the world’s sharpest AI-induced swings because it’s dominated by two tech giants, Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix. World.title: ‘Don’t call it a rebel league’: Inside surfing’s new $20m Big Bash-style comp
World.content:
SportSurfing ‘Don’t call it a rebel league’: Inside surfing’s new $20m Big Bash-style comp Dan Walsh August 19, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

An ambitious “made for TV” summer surfing league will launch with the promise of career-changing $10,000 weekly wages for Australian surfers on the basis of team franchises being sold to cover the competition’s estimated $20 million running costs. The Surfing Super League (SSL), a nine-week “home-and-away” season to be contested by eight teams along the east coast of Australia from January 2028, has been unveiled by majority owner and former Surfing Australia chief executive Chris Mater. Owen Wright (left) will come out of competitive retirement to compete in the Surfing Super League, a new venture led by CEO and founder Chris Mater. Sam Mooy The breakaway league is pitching as an alternative to traditional one-on-one professional surfing formats, which feature multi-week, condition-based competition windows at world-class waves. Instead, the SSL will feature teams of four surfers contesting a 90-minute, relay-based event in fixed Saturday and Sunday afternoon timeslots across school holidays.



The league aims to offer guaranteed broadcast content regardless of conditions in what are traditionally less reliable summer months for quality waves and swell, at spectator-friendly beach venues. Surfing Australia, the sport’s governing body domestically, is not involved in the start-up league. Surfing Australia representatives could not be reached for comment. Olympic bronze medallist Owen Wright, big-wave record-holder Laura Enever and former world No.2 Bede Durbidge have signed on as the competition’s biggest names, which will target “out-of-market” domestic and international surfers, along with Australia’s next generation rather than established surfers already competing on the WSL’s Championship Tour. Documents registered with the Australian Securities and Investments Commission show the SSL was initially valued at approximately $13.53 million based on the $483,333 seed investment for a 3.6 per cent stake by David Elsworth, an Australian entrepreneur whose background includes high-level marketing roles with Coca-Cola in Japan and ownership of a Japanese gin distillery and pet care company.



The league’s valuation has since been marked as significantly higher. Mater is confident of locking in a broadcast partner as negotiations with DAZN, owners of subscription platform Kayo, continue, while free-to-air providers Nine, Seven and Ten have also been approached. Mater will now begin a market search for a principal partner and sponsors for each of the eight franchises. In total, Mater predicts running the start-up league will cost “north of $20 million in season one”, with $89,000 wages for 48 surfers (each franchise will have a squad of six, four men and two women) amounting to more than $4.2 million in salaries alone. Marketed as “the Big Bash of surfing” with a nod to cricket’s T20 format and franchise-based competitions, SSL’s business modelling projects for two of the eight teams to be sold to private investors in order to turn a profit after its first season.



“I wouldn’t call this a rebel league at all,” Mater told this masthead. “I think it’s a complementary league [to the WSL’s world tour]. Or I would ask, is the V8 Supercars a rebel league? This is a format Australian surfing needs. We’re not trying to compete with the WSL. “There’s a big gap in the domestic market given pro surfing focuses on the international stage, and the national bodies focus on junior development. “But what we’re doing is creating a real ‘made for TV’ event, and a pathway for Australian surfers to compete in a very different format that opens surfing up in a new way to broadcasters and fans”. The SSL’s January-February season would land in the WSL’s off-season as well as a window between cricket’s Test schedule and the NRL and AFL seasons. “It’s going to change lives for the next generation”: Owen Wright. Sam Mooy



The new venture’s format and schedule will, however, potentially collide with Surfing Australia’s own teams-based Boardrider Battle, which runs across seven east coast events before a grand final in March. By locking events into specific summer timeslots, though, SSL organisers risk surfers regularly competing in blown-out, poor quality waves. “And if you’re in a traditional one-on-one surfing heat, you cannot run an event in poor surf,” Mater said. “There’s too much of surfers waiting around, it’s just deadset boring. The teams format adds an ironman element where you’re racing the clock with 40 minutes to get your surfers in and out of the water, catching as many waves as they need to win the game. Former WCT surfer Sophie McCulloch has signed on with the Surfing Super League. Andrew Shield



“It’s a really dynamic format that allows us to run in less than ideal conditions.” The proposed $89,000 contracts for all SSL surfers, regardless of gender or competition status, are a significant selling point given the gulf between surfing’s elite and athletes on the world tour’s fringe and below. Super Surf League founder and majority share-holder Chris Mater. Sam Mooy Surfers like reigning world champion Molly Picklum and leading Australian men Jack Robinson and Ethan Ewing hold non-compete clauses in their WSL contracts, which require express permission for them to compete in other events, and as a result, are not being targeted by SSL. “The kind of money we’re talking about for more than a handful of Australian surfers here is unheard of,” Wright said.



“It’s going to change lives for the next generation. It can help someone pursue a professional career, and take a real run at the WCT with all the travel and costs that involves. The market around things like individual sponsors is really shifting, so that’s a big reason why I’m so passionate about this format”. Mater resigned as Surfing Australia chief executive in late-2025 after seven years in charge and describes the sport as “one of the country’s most powerful untapped commercial opportunities”. He believes grassroots investment and under 18s and under 21s competitions around each regional franchise will help create genuine fan engagement and in turn, attract private investors. “We’ll run the league in the first season and our model is budgeting for at the end of that first season, we’ll have proven it’s successful with crowds, TV ratings and our events,” Mater said. “We’ll then be selling two of the eight teams. And each season we’re going to sell another two, plan to introduce two more franchises by season five and create a big engine of revenue and profit on top of a model that already takes in sponsors, ticketing, merchandise and a diversified revenue stream.” News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday.

World.title: ‘Meta needed kids’: Tech giant on trial over social media addiction
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaSocial media ‘Meta needed kids’: Tech giant on trial over social media addiction Diana Novak Jones and Jonathan Stempel Updated August 19, 2026 — 5:37am ,first published 3:20am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Meta Platforms intentionally sought to addict children to its Facebook and Instagram platforms in pursuit of profit, a lawyer for California said on Tuesday (US time) at the start of a trial that could reshape some of the most popular apps on the planet. A bipartisan group of 29 US states is suing Meta, seeking potentially tens or hundreds of billions of dollars in penalties and changes to how Meta does business. Loading Four lead states – California, Colorado, Kentucky and New Jersey – accuse Meta of designing Facebook and Instagram to hook young users, fuelling anxiety, depression and even suicide, and misleading consumers about the platforms’ safety. Jurors will hear claims by all 29 states that Meta violated federal law by improperly collecting and using personal data of children while they used its platforms.



Megan O’Neill, a deputy attorney general for California, told an eight-person jury in her opening statement that Meta’s business model was to “hook the users, hold them for as long as they can, harvest their data, and then hide the truth from the public.” “It worked especially well for kids,” O’Neill added. “Meta needed kids, and it needed to reassure the people who cared about those kids that the kids are safe.” The Ronald V. Dellums Federal Building and US Courthouse in Oakland, California. Bloomberg Meta’s lawyer Paul Schmidt countered in his opening statement that the company and its co-founder and chief executive Mark Zuckerberg shared a desire to improve their services, not to make them dangerous. “They don’t believe they’re going to do well if people don’t like their service,” Schmidt said.



Jurors in the Oakland, California, federal court are expected to issue an advisory verdict, but US District Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers will determine Meta’s liability. Related Article Social media Meta and Google found liable in landmark social media addiction trial If she finds Meta liable, Rogers could impose civil penalties and order changes to Facebook and Instagram. Meta has said it did not make misleading statements about safety, and the states failed to show their residents were harmed. Zuckerberg and Instagram chief Adam Mosseri are expected to testify. The trial is scheduled to last six weeks.



Experts have said the trial is the biggest legal test yet of social media’s effects on young users, and comes amid a broader reckoning across the globe over those effects. Meta has said penalties could be as high as $US1.4 trillion ($1.97 trillion), close to the Menlo Park, California-based company’s market value. California Attorney General Rob Bonta arrives at the courthouse on Tuesday. AP Photo/Noah Berger Attorneys general have yet to specify penalties but said at a hearing last week the amount could be closer to $US200 billion ($282 billion) – equivalent to about three years of after-tax profit for Meta. California, Colorado, Kentucky and New Jersey also want Meta to implement age restrictions, and eliminate the infinite scroll that encourages users to keep looking at new posts.



O’Neill said the states were not trying to put Meta, or social media, out of business. “This case is not about whether social media has some benefits for some people. It does,” she said. Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, pictured in February, is expected to give evidence. Bloomberg But she said Meta exploited children for its own benefit, researching how children’s brains work and would react to online stimuli, and tracking every interaction that children had on its apps. She showed jurors an internal email sent to Mosseri, which said “teen time spent” was the company’s goal, and said Meta employees viewed Instagram as a “drug” and themselves as “pushers”.



“Meta found the younger a kid is when they start using the app, the better,” O’Neill said. “The more likely they are to remain a user, the more likely they are to make Meta money in the long run.” Related Article Online gambling Facebook is advertising illegal gambling, and the watchdog is powerless to stop it Schmidt acknowledged that employees might use “loose” language in private, but jurors would hear what the employee who called Instagram a drug then did to make it safer. Some critics of Meta spoke outside the courthouse as the trial began. Among them was Mary Rodee, who said her 15-year-old son Riley Basford was victimised by a predator on Facebook before he died by suicide in 2021.



“They call it spontaneous suicide,” she said. “I call it what it was, the predictable outcome of a system that protects corporations instead of children.” The lawsuit began in 2023, two years after whistleblower Frances Haugen testified to a US Senate committee that Meta knew its products were unsafe for children and knew how to fix the problem, but did nothing in favour of pursuing higher profits. Meta and other social media companies including Snap, TikTok parent ByteDance and YouTube parent Alphabet face thousands of lawsuits by states, municipalities, school districts and individuals over whether their products harm young users. In March, a Los Angeles jury ordered Meta and Google to pay $US6 million to a 20-year-old woman who said she became addicted to Instagram and YouTube media as a child. Earlier this month, a New Mexico judge ordered Meta to pay $US567 million into a mental health fund for teenagers after that state’s attorney general said the company’s platforms were a public nuisance.

World.title: Flu wards set up, elective surgery cancelled as hospital admissions surge
World.content:
Influenza spike sees Covid-style measures return Morning Report Download MP3 5m

Hospitals have created dedicated flu wards and some elective surgery is being cancelled, as influenza A hits the health system hard.

Health bosses were now meeting daily to monitor the situation and keep an eye on hospital capacity across the country, with the upper North Island most affected.

Nurses said Health NZ was not doing enough and front-line health staff were struggling to cope.

Over the past two weeks, the number of patients turning up to emergency departments had increased and, in the first week of August, flu admissions doubled.

Health NZ winter planning lead Chris Lowry said flu-only wards helped keep others safe.

"If we aggregate people together, that helps stop any internal spread, when you might have them scattered through a ward... even if they are in isolation."

She was not able to name all the hospitals that had dedicated flu wards, but said they tended to be larger hospitals.

Health NZ winter planning lead Chris Lowry said flu-only wards helped keep others safe. RNZ

As well as the daily meeting, Health NZ had set up a national co-ordination centre to help with planning and support any areas that needed it , Lowry said.

Each hospital had 'flex beds' that could move to where they were most needed, as part of Health NZ's winter plan, released in April with a promise to help ease pressure, but the NZ Nurses Organisation is asking where that plan is.

Delegate and Waikato Hospital emergency department nurse Tracey Chisholm said there was very little sign of it - including the extra beds.

'Bed block' - where patients became stuck in the emergency department, because there was no space for them in a hospital ward - was still happening, she said. That contributed to regular wait-times of 10 hours or more.

Lowry said the planned flex beds were not always available, partly because winter illness was also taking out the nurses who would staff them, but the union said Health NZ should have addressed chronic understaffing.

A really 'yuck' strain

Many general practices were also separating patients with flu-like symptoms.

NZ College of General Practitioners president Luke Bradford said some were holding dedicated respiratory clinics or seeing patients with flu symptoms in a different space to others.

NZ College of General Practitioners president Luke Bradford is taking his own advice this week, because of flu-like symptoms. Supplied

Those who ended up in hospital tended to have either developed secondary infections, such as pneumonia, had complicating conditions, or were unwell from high fevers or dehydration, he said.

"Every so often, you get a strain of flu that is just yuck, that does makes people feel particularly unwell, and I think that's what we've got this year. It does seem to have come quickly, as the peak's ramped up very fast."

Doctors at the top of the North Island had particularly noticed big numbers through the doors, with the peak appearing to hit later than the South Island, he said.

Bradford was following his own advice this week, staying home and away from a planned gathering, because of flu-like symptoms.

"I wrote myself a list of chores and then have failed to get any of them done, so I've actually sat on the sofa with some Panadol and fluids and a cup of tea, and been watching some streaming programmes," he said

Anyone with flu should rest and hydrate, and contact their doctor, if they were worried, or had shortness of breath, chest pain, a worsening fever or felt very unwell.

Lowry said anyone who needed to go to an emergency department should always go, and they would be seen and well cared for.

World.title: Morning Report: Nicola Willis and Carmel Sepuloni talk tax on RNZ's political panel
World.content:
Weekly Political Panel: Nicola Willis and Carmel Sepuloni Morning Report Download MP3 15m

National has the pressure on Labour to announce which taxes it will take to the campaign, and be open to from its potential coalition partners.

Finance spokesperson Nicola Willis on Sunday called for Labour leader Chris Hipkins to clarify his position on taxing on streaming companies such as Netflix or bringing back the so-called ute tax.

Chris Hipkins ruled out both, before realising a bill that would have taxed streaming companies was still in the ballot.

Labour has since ditched the member's bill blaming an administrative oversight.
