World.title: Christopher Luxon, Chris Bishop press fondness for Hutt Valley in show of party unity
World.content:
Luxon turns out for Bishop in Lower Hutt electorate Morning Report Download MP3 3m

Prime Minister Christopher Luxon and Chris Bishop - one of his ministers accused of trying to topple him last week - were all smiles at a public meeting in the latter's electorate on Tuesday night.

Leadership squabbles escaped any mention, with just one veiled reference to politics being a "tough sport" in opening remarks.

"It's a rough game, we know that."

About 250 people turned out on a wet Tuesday evening the Fraser Park Events centre in Avalon, Lower Hutt where a brick near the entrance is adorned with the words: Chris Bishop MP for Hutt South.

It's a title the Attorney-General, Minister for Housing, Infrastructure and Transport will want to retain in this year's election - particularly given a combination of low polling and high numbers of electorate wins could turf him out of Parliament altogether.

Bishop praised his party leader, calling Luxon the man in charge of National's plan who was doing "an outstanding job".

National leader Christopher Luxon at the podium at the Fraser Park Events centre in Avalon in Lower Hutt. Sanele Chadwick/RNZ

He said Luxon had got into politics and Parliament for the right reasons, "dedicating his life to public service to try and make a difference for all of us".

Luxon in turn gave acknowledgement to "the great Chris Bishop".

"If you cut him, he bleeds the Hutt. That's what he believes. He eats, breathes, sleeps it. He's talking about it every Tuesday in our caucus room.

"So, mate, thank you for your public service because you've been a dedicated public servant and representative for this region for some time," he said, later praising his third-ranked MP for his work on the Resource Management Act reforms.

Luxon's speech warned the world was at an "inflection point" of mass change.

"Turn on the six o'clock news and you see things like countries that used to be friends with each other actually squabbling and fighting ... wars in Ukraine in the middle of Europe, but also in the Middle East, we see trade wars flaring between countries that we thought were friends and alliance partners.

"We had a similar experience after World War I; after World War II; certainly after the fall of the [Berlin] Wall in 1989; and I put it to you, since 2024. The world has been changing in terms of how it deals with each other and works together or doesn't."

He pitched himself as an "outside politician" who had "watched them for years just boil the ocean, lots of bumper stickers, lots of promises", when people wanted "delivery".

Several questions Luxon answered effectively but with the usual party lines, or asking audience members to "watch this space" for future party policy announcements.

Chris Bishop and Christopher Luxon arrive at the meeting. Sanele Chadwick/RNZ

FENZ in firing line

Perhaps the most heated was about why - given Labour sorted union negotiations out with firefighters after the first ever nationwide strike - National hasn't done the same after 54; and why a community centre burned down about 550 metres from the previous fire station that got shut down.

Bishop said Fire and Emergency (FENZ) was a "shocker" at managing their assets.

"I have been pushing them and the Minister of Internal Affairs, Brooke van Velden, very hard to say what is the plan around the Hutt City fire station, and I just get crickets in response because you've got an incompetent governence and management there ... I'm furious about it."

Luxon said the "bottom line is, they have money. They have enough money".

About 250 people turned out on a wet night to listen to the two politicians. Sanele Chadwick/RNZ

The prime minister refused to commit to not lowering funding for kindergartens, but again said there would be more policy to come.

When asked how National could help conservative voices in local government to oppose Labour and Green councillors, Luxon said "if only 30 percent of you bother to vote in a local body election, you kind of get what you deserve".

In response to questions about removing climate change from curriculums, he said the first thing was getting kids to school, then teaching them to read and do maths, before giving them the foundations to engage in science and climate change.

Bishop kept the last question for himself to ask Luxon about his connection to the Hutt Valley, saying few people may know he began at Unilever in Petone.

"I am a Crusaders supporter, you know that and we've just lost the whole room now," Luxon quipped.

"That business, they had a big factory down the bottom end of Jackson Street and so I came here as the brand manager for Sunlight dishwash liquid, Jif cream cleanser and Handy Andy ... as a 22, 24 year old.

"It was an amazing place to live, and I'm really grateful for the start that business gave me, but also the city gave me that then led me to live overseas for 16 years doing some other things with that same business."

He finished with a joke about hearing a "massive rumble" after moving to Sydney and getting under his desk thinking it was an earthquake, but the Australian marketing director said it was just a truck from the factory.

Luxon and Bishop then spoke to those in attendance and took selfies for about another half hour.

Those in attendance had mixed views of the discussion, with some National supporters saying it was great, and good to hear from the prime minister with full context rather than in soundbites.

Several undecided voters who spoke to RNZ remained unconvinced, saying their votes had not been swayed at all.

World.title: Changes for how endometriosis is diagnosed could be 'a big win'
World.content:
Clinical guidelines for endometriosis diagnoses are changing Morning Report Download MP3 5m

Changes on the way for how endometriosis is diagnosed offer hope for those living with the painful condition, Endometriosis NZ chief executive Tanya Cooke said.

New clinical guidelines announced on Tuesday will mean general practitioners can make a diagnosis based on symptoms and examination, rather than waiting for a laparoscopy.

The change puts a greater reliance on imaging, rather than surgery, Cooke said.

"So people who are suffering from the condition will receive a diagnosis much earlier and can commence treatment and this should make a big difference."

The average wait for diagnosis is currently nearly 10 years, and patients live with significant pain, she said.

Endometriosis is an inflammatory disease where tissue similar to the lining of the uterus grows outside it. Symptoms include period and pelvic pain, subfertility and infertility.

"You cannot underestimate what people go through when they're experiencing these debilitating symptoms. Young girls have to take time off school, maybe can't take on the careers that they wanted to," Cooke said.

"It can have a huge impact on somebody's quality of life. So there's hope that we can get on top of the diagnosis early and really improve the outcomes for the minimum of 120,000 people that are living with endometriosis here in New Zealand."

She said the change is "a big win" for those living with the condition.

"It's been an accumulation of sustained advocacy from our organisation, but we're excited to have international clinical best practice implemented here in New Zealand."

The gold standard for diagnosis has been surgery, which the new guidelines move away from towards updates in imaging, such as transvaginal ultrasounds and potentially MRIs, Cooke said.

Announcing the changes on Tuesday, Health Minister Simeon Brown said once a clinical diagnosis is made, GPs will then be able to prescribe treatment immediately,

The change would mean low impact hormonal medication could be prescribed without delay, which Brown said was effective for up to 60 percent of patients.

Laparoscopic surgery would remain available for those who needed it, but it would no longer be the only route to diagnosis.

Health NZ will adapt the Australian Living Evidence Guideline on Endometriosis for use in New Zealand, in collaboration with the Royal Australian and NZ College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists, other medical colleges and Endometriosis NZ.

World.title: Growing homelessness linked to tighter emergency housing rules, community leader says
World.content:
Did emergency housing clampdown cause homelessness spike? Morning Report Download MP3 8m

A community housing leader says there is a direct link between growing homelessness and the government's decision to tighten emergency housing eligibility.

However, the responsible minister says the stricter criteria were implemented along with increased support for those in need.

In recent times, about a third of emergency housing applications to the Ministry of Social Development are being declined each month, according to the agency's latest figures released to RNZ under the Official Information Act.

Before August 2024 - when stricter rules about getting into and staying in emergency housing came into force - decline rates were in the single digits.

That came a few months after the Government set a target to reduce the number of households in emergency housing by 75 percent, saying motels weren't appropriate for families, especially children.

Community Housing Aotearoa chief executive Paul Gilberd said the data spoke for itself.

"One can clearly see the policy direction, the moment in time when the policy direction to the MSD staff was changed, the steep and significant decline in emergency and special needs grants, and the corresponding increase in rough sleeping around the country."

Gilberd said while there was "a lot of debate" about exact homelessness figures, data gathered by community groups showed "it's at the highest level it has ever been".

He said there was consensus that children should not grow up in emergency housing motels, but reducing their use had left some without alternatives.

"It's a lose-lose scenario for everybody who is involved. It's not great for the staff at MSD. It's definitely not a great outcome for our rough sleeping and homeless communities, and it's not a really good outcome for taxpayers because where they're ending up is in the emergency departments and in Corrections."

Paul Gilberd RNZ / Edward O'Driscoll

MSD figures from June show the most common reason for declining emergency housing applications is "the need can be met another way" (about 27 percent of 729 rejections), followed by "you have caused or contributed to your immediate need" (about 19 percent).

The latter category was among several new criteria introduced in mid-2024, intended to "tighten the gateway" to emergency housing.

MSD officials told ministers at the time the changes risked increasing homelessness, particularly for children, Māori, and people with complex needs.

However, unlike other criteria, Ministers decided MSD staff should have discretion about whether to apply the "caused or contributed to your immediate need" test to an applicant.

"An option considered was making 'contribution to immediate EH [emergency housing] need' a compulsory consideration. However, this determination is a subjective assessment, and can risk excluding people with an immediate EH need, exacerbating support needs and therefore creating a long-term fiscal cost," the report read.

Gilberd described determining whether someone contributed to their homelessness as "deeply problematic", as it required frontline staff to make subjective decisions with imperfect information.

"We know that our rough sleepers and homeless, who have typically had quite a bad experience of life and of agencies, are deeply reluctant to be fully clear and transparent and share all of their personal information when they walk into an MSD office and meet a case manager."

In March, an Auditor-General report into housing needs recommended MSD staff guidance be updated to ensure assessments about "contributing" to one's need for emergency housing be clarified - something the agency had since done.

Gilberd said the core issue was the lack of affordable housing due to underinvestment by successive governments.

He said he was agnostic about who would supply that housing - be it Kāinga Ora, community housing providers, iwi, or churches.

"Until we decide as a society and give the signals to our politicians that it's going to be safe for them to get re-elected by having a policy which invests significant additional new money into this supply, this problem is not going to go away."

Associate Housing Minister Tama Potaka RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

Potaka: Emergency housing changes appropriate

Associate Housing Minister Tama Potaka said the government's tightening of emergency housing grants in 2024 "restored emergency housing to its purpose as a last resort".

He said the changes came alongside increased support for people with housing needs, as well as more public and transitional housing.

"Our Government has always wanted, and continues to want, people to have a safe and secure roof over their heads, not to be left living in a hotel room," Potaka said in a statement.

"Emergency housing was never intended to become a long-term home for thousands of families. We set a target to reduce the number of households in emergency housing by 75 percent by 2030, and achieved it five years early."

He said about 70 percent of those not granted emergency housing were offered alternative support, such as transitional housing, help to remain in their current home, or assistance securing a private rental.

As for the remaining 30 percent, Potaka told the Herald in June: "Some of those people may well be in housing now, some of them may not be."

Potaka says the government "restored emergency housing to its purpose as a last resort". RNZ / Rayssa Almeida

Meanwhile, MSD told RNZ last month people were under no obligation to tell the agency where they were living.

Karen Hocking, MSD's enablement group general manager, said emergency housing applications were most often declined when applicants had other options available, such as staying with family or friends.

"We may also decline someone's application if their situation is a result of their own actions, or actions of people they are responsible for, and they were reasonably able to predict and prevent it," she said in a statement.

"For example, people are generally expected to organise somewhere new to live before they leave their existing accommodation. If someone chooses to give up their tenancy without a good reason and without making other arrangements, they are likely to have unreasonably caused or contributed to their immediate need."

Hocking said people leaving their homes due to family violence would not be considered to have contributed to their need.

World.title: Dairy prices rally at latest global auction amid threat of El Niño disruption
World.content:
Milk prices across several commodities have risen at the latest Global Dairy Trade auction.

The average price rose almost 2.3 percent overnight to US$3873(NZ$6597). It followed prices holding steady at the last auction with just a 0.1 percent price increase two weeks ago.

In a note, New Zealand Exchange dairy analyst Rosalind Crickett said it was another bullish result for most dairy commodities.

"Sentiment in the market over the last couple of weeks remains centred around the same thing," she said.

"While global milk production may have been strong in the year-to-date out of most regions, record high temperatures in the Northern Hemisphere, paired with the potentially strongest El Niño weather on record for the Southern Hemisphere in the months to come, could change the supply side dynamic."

Adding to this, she said it was a key time for buyers to get orders over the line ahead of the festive season.

Last week Fonterra lifted its 12-month butter volumes forecast by 4.7 percent. 123rf

The important whole-milk powder price rose 3 percent to US$3591 (NZ$6116). It was the same for skim milk powder which rose 7.6 percent, hovering near12-month highs seen in May this year.

Crickett said this was "in line with expectations" as there were concerns about future milk production.

"While Europe and the US most recent data showed continued growth, reports on the ground are depicting farmers are already starting to dip into winter feed reserves amid drought conditions."

Butter meanwhile was down 2 percent, and anhydrous milk fat was down 6 percent- attributed to ample global supply of milk fats.

Last week Fonterra lifted its 12-month butter volumes forecast by 4.7 percent, while US butter was production up 8.5 percent year on year in June and Europe's rose 5.4 percent in May.

World.title: New mum returns to international 'murderball' with blunt new perspective
World.content:
For Ella Sabljak, the 2026 Wheelchair Rugby World Championships will be a little different to her tournament debut in Denmark four years earlier.

Sabljak, one of four women on the Australian Steelers' mixed-gender roster for the event, is making her return to international competition less than a year after giving birth to her first child.

Along for the ride is baby Billie, slotting into a non-playing but important morale-based role with the team, which has just begun its title defence in the Brazilian city of São Paulo.

Sabljak has returned to international competition accompanied by daughter Billie. (Supplied: Wheelchair Rugby Australia, Albin John)

And motherhood has given Sabljak a blunt new perspective.

"Back then [at the 2022 World Championships] you got to mess around a bit and have fun, where now I want to get in, I want to work hard, and I want to get out," Sabljak told ABC Sport after arriving in camp.

"I'm not into all the mess around like I used to be. If something's going to take up my time away from Billie, it's going to be worth it. She is my number one priority.

"Let's get in, let's f*** s*** up, and let's get out of here."

The road back to international competition

It has not been a straightforward journey back to the international arena for Sabljak, who says she would never have anticipated such a quick return to representative duties.

Only a visit from some of her Steelers teammates in the weeks after giving birth convinced her to return to the sport.

"I was at the stage of postpartum where I didn't know if I wanted to [come back] and they just planted the seed around returning to sport," Sabljak said.

Sabljak was a bronze medallist with the Steelers at the 2024 Paralympics. (Getty Images: Alex Davidson)

But working off a tailored, week-by-week plan, Sabljak plotted her return to elite international competition, all while breastfeeding and working her day job.

Her involvement at the 2026 tournament comes 11 months after Billie's birth, and it is a feat Sabljak never would have thought possible in the immediate aftermath of becoming a mother.

"Not a chance [did I expect to be at the tournament]," she said.

"I thought about it and then we just kind of joked about it, and I was like, 'That's not going to happen! We've got a baby. We've got a small human we need to care for!'"

Bond (left) and Sabljak (right) will line-up for the Steelers at this week's Wheelchair Rugby World Championships in Brazil. (Supplied: Wheelchair Rugby Australia, Albin John)

But Sabljak has felt right at home bringing Billie into the Steelers' camp, with several of her teammates already parents themselves.

Captain Chris Bond, a 15-year veteran of the team with kids aged four and six, told ABC Sport Billie's presence in the camp has been "refreshing" for the whole team.

"We're not their parent, but we get to hang out with them and fulfil that part of us when we're away from our own kids," Bond said.

"It brings out the human side of our team. We are athletes, and we're going to do a job.

"But at the end of the day we're people, and we're humans, and we've got lives outside of sport, and the closer we can connect as people and friends and humans, the better connection we have on court as athletes."

Transitioning to a full-throttle, mixed-gender sport

Wheelchair rugby is known for its big hits and uncompromising physicality. (Getty Images: Alex Pantling)

Previously known by the rather foreboding moniker "murderball", wheelchair rugby is a full-contact sport, renowned for its big hits and end-to-end action.

It does not resemble either rugby code much, with a circular ball permitted to be thrown in any direction.

And unusually for elite-level international sport, it is contested by mixed-gender teams.

Women have traditionally had little representation at the highest level, but a recent rejigging of classification rules as well as a top-down, institutional emphasis on expanding female pathways within the sport have aimed at changing that.

However, questions remain over the long-term viability of the mixed-gender model, with one study in 2025 finding only 2.2 per cent of wheelchair rugby players internationally to be female.

The Steelers are the exception, having focused on increasing female representation over the past few years.

Do you have a story idea about women in sport? Email us abcsport5050@your.abc.net.au

There are four women in the squad for the 2026 World Championships, accounting for a third of the team.

Bond says the increase in female representation has coincided with a positive cultural shift for the Steelers, who have been the standard-bearers for international competition in the modern era, winning two World Championship titles and two Paralympic golds since 2012.

He says the "rough and tumble, blokey culture" has transformed and the players now "accept anyone for who they are".

For Sabljak, who was a Paralympian in wheelchair basketball before switching codes in 2022, the transition to a mixed-gender sport had its challenges.

"The locker rooms are vastly different; an all-girls locker room versus a boys-dominant locker room is quite, quite different," Sabljak said.

"Just like the conversations that happen, the music that's being played."

Shae Graham became the first woman to represent the Steelers at a Paralympic Games at Tokyo 2020, and Sabljak said she would not have conceived of joining the team if it were not for Graham's breakthrough.

Graham (right) was a trailblazer for Australian women in wheelchair rugby. (ABC News: Patrick Stone)

Along with Sabljak and Graham, Emilie Miller is now a mainstay of the Steelers set-up, while Lilliana Prucha is making her World Championships debut in Brazil.

"[Having women in the team] is just the norm now, nobody questions it," Sabljak said.

While the Steelers are defending world champions, they enter this year's tournament with a point to prove, having claimed bronze at the 2024 Paralympics, the last major international meet.

That was the team's second-lowest finish across seven international tournaments since 2012, after placing fourth at Tokyo 2020.

Bond says the international standard has never been higher, with "six or seven" nations now serious contenders to finish atop the podium, but believes this Steelers side is "the strongest he's ever been a part of".

"I'm really excited about this team," Bond said.

"We've got so much more depth than we've ever had, we feel really good, really prepared, and the rest is up to the sporting gods."

World.title: AFL policy is to wait while police investigate. The Swans may not
World.content:
The Sydney Swans' declaration that some players are in "serious breach" of club standards has signalled a tougher approach after days of uncertainty over how the AFL would handle a report of an alleged incident at a Melbourne hotel where Swans players were staying.

Four Swans players — Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner, James Jordon and Riley Bice — are understood to be linked to a Victoria Police investigation regarding an alleged sexual assault at an East Melbourne hotel in the early hours of Monday morning.

While few details have been made public beyond the allegation itself, Victorian police are continuing to investigate.

It is not suggested that any of the four players are being accused of sexual assault.

It is not known what breaches of club conduct the club has found.

On Tuesday evening, the Swans issued a statement saying the club would discuss appropriate sanctions and penalties after it finalised interviews with "all players involved".

"We respect there is an ongoing investigation by Victoria Police and any actions we take are independent of this," the statement said.

"The club believes the players are in serious breach of expected club behaviour and standards, and it is appropriate to take firm action and highlight that any sanction we impose relates solely to those breaches.

"The Sydney Swans condemn all forms of abuse and disrespectful behaviour towards women."

Growing pressure on Swans, AFL

Until last night, the club and the league had said relatively little, prompting experts to question whether the AFL's policy of waiting for a criminal investigation to take place if police are involved is a strong enough position for a league that has publicly condemned violence against women.

Sydney Swans CEO Matthew Pavlich addressed the media on Monday. (ABC News)

Some of the limited comments from AFL leaders had also drawn criticism, including Swans CEO Matthew Pavlich's mention of the club's extreme disappointment that its players had "found themselves in this situation".

Former AFL Women's star Kate McCarthy was among those who challenged that framing, noting: "Players don't simply 'find themselves in situations."

Others, including Our Watch CEO Patty Kinnersly, observed some media commentary centred on finals season while sidelining the "the alleged sexual assault at the centre of this story".

"In the coverage to date we've seen examples of poor reporting that has centred on on-field consequences ahead of a serious, alleged crime," she said.

Advocates welcome new statements from Swans, AFL

The alleged sexual assault has raised questions about how the AFL deals with alleged incidents like this, or if the league is doing enough to prevent incidents in the first place.

Last night AFL CEO Andrew Dillon offered the league's first substantial statement on the alleged sexual assault, labelling the allegations as "serious" and "deeply concerning".

"While the matter remains under police investigation, it raises broader issues for our game and our responsibilities as a sport," he said.

" It is important that the police process is allowed to run its course. "

Respect Victoria's CEO Helen Bolton, who had earlier criticised the league for not coming out strongly enough, welcomed the fresh statements from the Swans and the AFL.

"I think it's really encouraging that both the club and the AFL have made some really clear and accountable statements about the alleged conduct," she said.

Respect Victoria CEO Helen Bolton had called for a strong response from the AFL. (ABC News: Steven Schubert)

But she said it was disappointing that those statements took so long.

She also stressed the need for a "parallel process" for the AFL to lead its own response to the allegations while the police process was underway, which she said was no different than any other workplace.

AFL investigations pause when police involved

At a policy level, the AFL's default position is to let a criminal investigation run its course when police are involved.

The league's Respect and Responsibility policy outlines that "an AFL investigation will wait until a police investigation has been concluded".

Dr Catherine Ordway describes the AFL's approach to allegations as reactive, not proactive. (Supplied)

Lawyer and sports integrity expert, UNSW scholar Catherine Ordway, described that policy approach as "reactive".

She said it was not in line with best practice across sporting codes, including internationally.

"The AFL waits for the criminal law process to be finalised before taking action against any players or officials," she said.

Dr Ordway said she thought the players should be stood down while a police or AFL investigation took place.

NRL no-fault stand down rule

Since 2019, the NRL has had a policy that if serious charges are laid against a player, the player is stood down while the process moves through the courts.

"There are some pros and cons of that, but I think in terms of fairness that's the right decision. There needs to be some strong messaging about how unacceptable violence is against women," Dr Ordway said.

Australia's two major football codes have different policies for responding to criminal investigations. (ABC News: Baz Ruddick)

Dr Ordway described it as a more "proactive" approach in line with Major League Baseball in the US and the English Cricket Board.

Our Watch, which has delivered educational programs to AFL clubs on gendered violence, said it would support the league adopting a similar rule to the NRL.

"When we're wanting to focus on creating cultures of safety for women, we would support the no-fault stand down that the NRL has done," CEO Ms Kinnersly said.

The NRL players association opposed the no-fault stand down policy when it was introduced.

Sydney Swans scheduled to meet overnight

AFL Players Association CEO James Gallagher was asked about the no-fault policy on Tuesday but did not say if any equivalent would be opposed by the players' union.

"What we've got here at the moment is allegations, and so I think part of it is understanding exactly what's happened. We should take the time with it to properly understand," he told Triple M.

The Sydney Swans said its board would meet overnight to determine appropriate penalties.

The ABC has contacted the AFL Players Association and the AFL for comment.

World.title: Sydney Swans say players 'in serious breach' of club standards
World.content:
The Sydney Swans say the players allegedly connected to an incident at a Melbourne hotel "are in serious breach of expected club behaviour and standards".

The ABC understands four players — Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner, James Jordon and Riley Bice — are linked to an investigation into an alleged assault at the Pullman Hotel in east Melbourne, where the Swans were staying, in the early hours of Monday morning.

It is not suggested that any of the four players are being accused of sexual assault.

Victoria Police is investigating, stating this morning that "the exact circumstances are yet to be established and … no one has been arrested or formally interviewed at this time".

The club said it interviewed all the players linked to the incident in Melbourne and concluded "firm action" should be taken relating to the breaching of club standards.

(Clockwise from top left) James Jordon, Chad Warner, Riley Bice and Isaac Heeney are understood to be linked to a sexual assault investigation. (ABC News/Getty Images)

"The club also acknowledges that these serious allegations impact others and their wellbeing must be paramount," a statement read.

"The Sydney Swans condemn all forms of abuse and disrespectful behaviour towards women. Any conduct that causes offence or harm to others is unacceptable and falls well short of our expectations. All women deserve to be respected and feel safe.

"We also want to acknowledge that the care and welfare of our AFLW athletes and staff is of the utmost importance to us as a club.

"They have been and will continue to be offered the support they require, and we acknowledge the impact these allegations have on our female athletes, staff members and the wider community."

Heeney, Warner, Bice and Jordon did not appear at Swans HQ with the rest of their team on Tuesday and were interviewed by the club off-site with lawyers present.

The Swans board also met Tuesday night to agree on club-imposed sanctions and penalties.

Focus should not be on 'football consequences' AFLW star turned broadcaster Kate McCarthy calls out members of the media focusing on how a police investigation linked to Sydney Swans players could affect the team's finals chances.

"Any further sanctions or decisions regarding the outcome of the police investigation would take place after that process is completed," the statement read.

"During this time, we will provide the appropriate support to the players involved in the incident, along with their partners and families.

"The Sydney Swans hold all players and staff at the club to high standards of behaviour and personal conduct. Representing this club carries significant responsibilities both on and off the field, and we expect those standards to be upheld at all times.

"Our focus remains on cooperating fully with the AFL and authorities, maintaining the integrity of the process, and upholding the high standards expected of everyone who represents this club."

'Deeply concerning' incident: AFL CEO

AFL chief executive Andrew Dillon said the allegations around the Swans were "deeply concerning", stressing that, regardless of the outcome of the police investigation, the incident raised wider concerns around the game.

"The conduct and serious allegations regarding Sydney Swans players are deeply concerning," he said in a statement.

Andrew Dillon said the effects on a club's season had no bearing on the seriousness of the allegations. (Getty Images: Mark Kolbe)

"While the matter remains under police investigation, it raises broader issues for our game and our responsibilities as a sport.

"The woman who made the report to police is entitled to privacy and care, and that should be respected.

"It is important that the police process is allowed to run its course."

Dillon alluded to discussions around the potential sanctions or distractions for the Swans and the potential impact that may have on the second-placed club heading into the AFL finals.

"Sexual assault allegations are serious, regardless of who is involved, what time of year it is, or what they may mean for a season," he said ahead of the team's final home-and-away game on Sunday.

"Our first question should not be what this means for a football club. It should be whether our actions match the standards we stand for and the community expects of us.

"As a sport, and as an industry, we are clear about the standards we expect and the values we stand for and the need to uphold them.

"Being clear about our standards also means being prepared to act when those standards are not met.

"Notwithstanding the ongoing police investigation, the AFL and the Sydney Swans will consider the broader conduct of the players as more information comes to light."

World.title: Focus should not be on 'football consequences' for Swans, ex-AFLW star says
World.content:
Former AFL Women's star Kate McCarthy has questioned the tone of some of the media coverage around an ongoing police investigation involving Sydney Swans players.

Four Swans players — Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner, James Jordon and Riley Bice — are understood to be linked to a Victoria Police investigation regarding an alleged sexual assault at the hotel where the team was staying on Sunday night.

"The exact circumstances are yet to be established and the investigation into the incident remains ongoing," Victoria Police said.

"Police spoke to a number of people at the hotel, however no-one has been arrested or formally interviewed at this time."

News of the allegations yesterday sent shock waves through the league, naturally filling the slates of news bulletins and AFL panel shows.

On Channel Seven's Agenda Setters, former Port Adelaide star Kane Cornes spoke from "the football point of view" of the issue, saying the players' lack of consideration for their teammates "is what makes [him] so angry".

(Clockwise from top left) James Jordon, Riley Bice, Chad Warner and Isaac Heeney. (ABC News/ Getty Images)

"This is where I get really angry from a football point of view," he said.

"When you're two weeks away from a finals series, when Dane Rampe has played in four losing grand finals and he's probably in bed at age 36 or at home right now going, 'This is my last chance, I'm 36, I had a chance to finish second and host another home final, give myself one last chance at winning a premiership'.

"[Jake] Lloyd's played in four losing grand finals, Heeney himself has played in three. … You'd think it would mean a bit more to Isaac Heeney ... on the eve of a finals series and put your teammates and your team in jeopardy."

Loading Instagram content

On Fox Footy, Melbourne great Garry Lyon said he did not want to "understate or downplay the seriousness of" the case, insisting he could "only really comment on the one side and that is football-related matters".

"The rest will sort themselves out and again, that's not to dismiss all parties involved in this, so let's get that on the table," he said.

"What we can discuss is the ramifications from a football point of view and this is an unmitigated disaster for the Sydney Swans and for the game.

"Those pictures on the eve of the AFL finals series with plain clothes [police] and police cars outside a hotel room one week out from the finals series is an absolute disaster."

McCarthy, now a commentator for Seven and Triple M, said focusing on "the football consequences" for the team caused by any potential sanctions or distractions sent the wrong message, particularly to girls and women.

Kate McCarthy says the focus should not be on "the football consequences" of the police investigation. (Getty Images: Hancock)

The former Lion, Saint and Hawk also took issue with Swans chief executive Matthew Pavlich saying the club was "extremely shocked and disappointed that this has taken place and that the players have found themselves in this situation".

"AFL players occupy positions of enormous influence. We celebrate them as role models when they do wonderful things in the community, we can't suddenly decide they're 'just footballers' when difficult questions about behaviour, attitudes towards women and culture arise," she wrote on Instagram.

"Language matters too. Players don't simply 'find themselves in situations'. Adults have agency and make choices. Whatever this investigation ultimately determines, our language shouldn't inadvertently remove that agency or responsibility."

Current GWS player and McCarthy's former AFLW teammate, Tilly Lucas-Rodd, praised the post, while Lion star Jade Ellenger commented: "This is what using a platform for change looks like, so well said."

Loading...

The news about the Swans emerged two weeks after former AFL player-agent Ralph Carr was revealed as the "well-connected man" convicted of rape last month.

In the wake of that revelation, former player and Australian Football Hall of Fame member Sam Newman questioned the evidence in the case and said the victim "might have buyer's remorse".

McCarthy questioned how much the AFL was doing to truly engage and include women and girls in footy spaces if someone like Newman remained in the hall of fame.

"We should be asking serious questions about what and who we continue to celebrate as a league," she wrote.

"The AFL says it wants women and girls to feel that football belongs to them. That has to mean more than having an AFLW competition or getting women through the gates. It means examining the culture around men in football, how women are spoken about and treated, and how our industry responds when serious allegations involving women arise.

"This isn't about declaring anyone guilty. That is for police and the courts. When women are potentially harmed, why are we so quick to focus on what it means for the men on the football field?"

World.title: Why Tallis Duncan could be the answer for Australia's World Cup shortage
World.content:
The South Sydney backline might be an unusual place to find the answer to Australia's second-row shortage for this year's World Cup but regardless of position the form of Rabbitohs tyro Tallis Duncan is fast becoming impossible to deny.

Of the backrowers who played in this year's Origin series only Liam Martin can be considered an automatic selection for Kevin Walters's squad.

Hudson Young and Dylan Lucas are both out with injuries, Haumole Olakau'atu will represent Tonga, Briton Nikora is already tied to New Zealand and Angus Crichton's status is uncertain amid his impending move to rugby.

Duncan has improved out of sight in the past 12 months. (Getty Images: Mark Metcalfe )

Duncan would have to beat out the likes of Canterbury's Jacob Preston and Warriors veteran Kurt Capewell, and Kulikefu Finefeuiaki, David Fifita and Heilum Luki will all be in the mix if they don't opt to represent Tonga and Samoa respectively, but the door is open for him to claim his first taste of higher honours.

The 24-year old has been a rare constant for South Sydney in a helter-skelter season, impressing at second row and in recent weeks at centre.

His effort against Canterbury last week, where Duncan scored a try, threw the final pass for another and ran for 182 metres from 23 carries, has become typical fare and with the Rabbitohs hitting form at just the right time, a strong finish to the season could well propel Duncan into a green and gold jersey.

Blues bash brothers unleash the beautiful crazy Liam Martin and Hudson Young don't like to point fingers unless it comes time to decide which of the New South Wales backrowers is madder.

"It's definitely something I've dreamed about my whole life. I haven't spoken about it too much publicly, that's not really the type I am," Duncan said.

"But that's a dream and if I was able to achieve that dream it would mean everything to me and my family. That's all I have to say about it now."

Injuries have forced Duncan to spend the last month at centre and while he's still just filling in out wide, that versatility would make him all the more valuable as part of Australia's squad.

That time out wide is only temporary but his success there is proof of Duncan's growing maturity.

He's improved out of sight compared to this time last year by leaning on the experience of players like Jack Wighton and the injured Latrell Mitchell, who have both played centre for New South Wales and Australia.

"I'm a second-rower, but being able to help the team in any way, I'll always put my hand up for that," Duncan said.

"I want to be part of an environment that's team first and for me to want that I have to live that. I believe we're doing that now.

"I've got a lot of good centres around me at training and I'm not too proud to ask for help."

Duncan also believes an increase in trust between himself, South Sydney's ageless wonder Cody Walker and Alex Johnston, who Duncan cites as key to identifying opposition shapes, as a key to his recent success.

The Rabbitohs have hit form at just the right time. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor )

At the time of writing he has as many tries this season as the Dolphins' Herbie Farnworth, the best centre in the league, and he's first in the league among backrowers for line breaks and second for tackle busts.

"I try to have intent in what I do and I pride myself on running hard lines," Duncan said.

"I know how hard it is to defend someone when they're running genuine leads, it just puts the defence under pressure.

"Everyone has a job to do and if I do mine then I'll get the ball because we've got quality ball-players like Cody and Duff (Matt Dufty)."

If the Rabbitohs' showing against Canterbury is anything to go by, Duncan will get more than a few chances to push his claims for an Australian jersey.

Wayne Bennett's side produced their best performance of the season to all but secure their top eight spot with a series of try-saving efforts the highlight of the 22-6 victory.

"I'm really proud of that one. We saved three tries before we scored one, that's what the good teams do," Duncan said.

"We might not seem like a team that prides themselves on defence but that's what we've been working on, so it's good to see the fruits of it.

"Good teams don't make errors in their own half, but when they do they defend them. We can be very proud of that."

World.title: Weatherald dropped from Test squad after stunning loss to Bangladesh
World.content:
Opening batter Jake Weatherald has been dropped from Australia's Test squad after the side's historic loss to Bangladesh in Darwin.

Matt Renshaw has been called into the 13-player squad for the second Test at Great Barrier Reef Stadium in Mackay, which begins on Saturday.

Weatherald made 23 and a third-ball duck in Australia's stunning nine-wicket loss to Bangladesh.

Shock loss to Bangladesh reveals Aussie cracks On paper, Australia's full-strength team should have wiped the floor with Bangladesh. But a lack of application to their Test match craft has left Australia vulnerable to teams that are driven to succeed in the longest format.

The Darwin-born top-order batter made his debut during last summer's Ashes series against England.

He averages 20.36 from his 12 innings in Test cricket, with a highest score of 72.

Renshaw, 30, now firms as Travis Head's opening partner for the second Test.

Renshaw played 11 Tests between 2016 and 2018, before being dropped from the side.

He was recalled to the side in 2023, when he played three Tests.

Renshaw has a highest Test score of 184, which he scored against Pakistan at the SCG in 2017.

Under-fire Marnus Labuschagne has kept his spot in the squad despite struggling for form in recent times.

Labuschagne scored 1 and 31 in his two innings in Darwin, and has not scored a century in his previous 22 Tests, averaging 25.23 in that time.

Coach Andrew McDonald said after the first-Test loss the changes to his technique had held up well, but warned Labuschagne "needs big runs".

He was not so complimentary of Weatherald.

"There was some change to Jake in terms of where he lined up and his movement patterns," the coach said.

"It's always hard to critique small sample sizes on whether it holds up. He dragged one on and drove at one in the first innings and was dismissed.

"It is probably harder with that smaller sample size to say, 'yep, that's going to hold up under pressure'."

Australia squad: Pat Cummins (c), Scott Boland, Alex Carey, Cameron Green, Josh Hazlewood, Travis Head, Josh Inglis, Marnus Labuschagne, Nathan Lyon, Matthew Renshaw, Steve Smith, Mitchell Starc, Beau Webster

Bangladesh squad: Najmul Hossain Shanto (c), Mehidy Hasan Miraz (vc), Soumya Sarkar, Shadman Islam, Tanzid Hasan Tamim, Mominul Haque Showrab, Mushfiqur Rahim, Litton Das, Amite Hasan, Jaker Ali Anik, Taijul Islam, Taskin Ahmed, Hasan Mahmud, Syed Khaled Ahmed, Ebadot Hossain Chowdhury, Musfik Hasan, Litton Das, Shoriful Islam

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

ABC/AAP

World.title: De Minaur advances to final 16 at Cincinnati in US Open warm-up event
World.content:
Alex de Minaur has seen off the rain and top-ranked Brit Arthur Fery to continue his campaign at the US Open warm-up event in Cincinnati.

The match was subject to three delays as the weather continued to play havoc with the schedule on Monday, but the fifth-seeded Australian overcame the disruptions to win 7-5, 7-6 (7-3) in two hours and 22 minutes.

Fery, who shot into the world's top 50 after reaching the Wimbledon semifinals at the All England Club as a wildcard, was playing his first match since Alexander Zverev ended that improbable run.

That catapulted the 24-year-old up the rankings to number 36 in the world, earning him a main draw second-round entry for the first time at an ATP 1000 Masters.

It nearly ended there at the Ohio tournament as another Australian, James Duckworth, put up a real fight before finally succumbing 6-4 2-6 7-6 (7-4).

De Minaur represented an even sterner challenge, though he was out of sorts early on, perhaps unsettled by an early rain break in his first service game, and had to save three break points in his next service game.

The match steadied until the 11th game when the world No.8 pounced, forcing a break point which he won with a firm drive that Fery returned into the net.

De Minaur then held to love to take the set, when the rain returned.

Upon resumption, the Aussie broke twice for a 5-1 lead before crumbling trying to serve it out, and the contest was tied at 5-5.

But the 'Demon' got it done in the tiebreaker to set up a last-16 showdown with either ninth-seeded Czech Jiri Lehecka or 21st seed Arthur Fils of France.

"I'm happy with the way I found a way. It got tough at the end, probably a little bit harder than it should have been," said de Minaur, who last reached the fourth round in Cincinnati in 2019.

"I played a very good match until the last rain delay, and then I had to dig deep. I had to kind of reset and take it one point at a time.

"I take confidence out of these types of tough wins, and hopefully every day I feel better and play better."

Compatriot Rinky Hijikata will not be joining de Minaur in round four after he was beaten 6-3, 6-4 by 14th seed Jakub Mensik.

Earlier, Rafael Jodar, Flavio Cobolli and Novak Djokovic's conqueror Thiago Agustin Tirante all won.

AAP with wires

World.title: Fraser named Carlton coach after leading Blues' AFL revival
World.content:
Carlton chief executive Graham Wright insists Josh Fraser's presentation alone would have been enough to guarantee his appointment as senior coach.

After a fairytale rise from 1-8 when Michael Voss exited as coach, Fraser was the unanimous choice to steer the Blues forward.

The former Collingwood and Gold Coast ruckman has won 10 of 13 games to guide Carlton into the most unlikely of finals appearances.

Sunday's draw against the Western Bulldogs sealed Carlton's spot in the top 10, with the club's board meeting to finalise Fraser's appointment on Monday.

Loading Instagram content

The results gave him the edge on untried assistants Jaymie Graham (Fremantle), Corey Enright (St Kilda) and James Kelly (Geelong), who all loomed strongly and presented to the coaching panel before Fraser did.

"Even if you removed the last 14 weeks, on his presentation alone Josh would have been the successful candidate," Wright said.

"Having run all candidates through a thorough and detailed process, for Josh to have emerged as the stand-out candidate speaks volumes of not only his credentials as a coach, but also the qualities he brings as a leader.

"He is a respectful whole-of-club leader who fosters a professional and united environment, with everyone contributing to our collective pursuit of excellence."

Even though he spent the majority of his playing career at the Magpies, Fraser's coaching journey has been largely at the old enemy.

The 44-year-old has had two stints as an assistant coach at Carlton, while also leading the club's VFL team.

When becoming interim coach, Fraser immediately ruled himself out of contention to stay in the role next year as a way to take pressure off the club.

"I have always had ambitions to be a senior coach and what the last three months have done is give me the absolute belief that I am ready, and most importantly ready for this exact opportunity, to be senior coach of the Carlton football club," Fraser said.

"When I was told that I had been appointed as senior coach, that sense of appreciation and responsibility I felt in that moment will never be lost on me.

"I firmly believe I am a product of amazing people around me.

"The collective commitment to each other and to get better every day in order to improve our football club is a privilege to be part of, and rest assured we want to continue to raise the standards in that regard."

AAP

Tech.title: Robin Williams’ Instagram account brought back to fight ‘AI abuse’
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Robin Williams’ children are taking over their father’s Instagram account after his daughter spoke out against the use of his AI likeness, as reported earlier by The Wrap. In a post on Tuesday, Zak, Zelda, and Cody Williams write that they want the late actor’s Instagram profile to be a “safe, trusted place where the stories, photos, videos, and memories shared reflect his legacy with authenticity, warmth, and care.”

A story posted to Zelda Williams’ own Instagram account expands on the decision to bring back her father’s profile, saying that it’s meant to help combat “rampant AI abuse,” according to The Wrap:

I’m sorry if anyone found Dad’s old page posting again to be triggering. Believe me, I know it’s a little strange. Making that space into one where people can find authentic clips and photos of him is one of the best ways we’ve now found to fight back against rampant AI abuse of his voice and likeness on here.

Robin Williams’ Instagram account remained inactive following his death in 2014. Last year, Zelda Williams asked fans to stop sending her AI-generated videos of her father. “To watch the legacies of real people be condensed down to ‘this vaguely looks and sounds like them so that’s enough’, just so other people can churn out horrible TikTok slop puppeteering them is maddening,” she wrote at the time.

Though some AI chatbots have restrictions in place to prevent users from generating images or videos with the AI likeness of a public figure or celebrity, these guardrails can still be bypassed. OpenAI’s now-shuttered Sora app became a hotbed for generating videos of copyrighted characters and celebrities, while Grok is still generating sexualized AI deepfakes of famous women, according to Wired.

Zelda, Zak, and Cody Williams add that they’re going to use their father’s Instagram account to share his “unique talent and humor with the world.”

Tech.title: OpenAI lays out new security changes after its AI hacked Hugging Face
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

OpenAI is announcing security updates following the July news that its AI broke out of a sandboxed environment and accidentally hacked Hugging Face, including improvements to its research environments, monitoring, and alignment techniques. The company had already put the brakes on a new model, Astra, that it thinks could have “critical” cybersecurity capabilities, and the company says it instituted a two-week pause in reinforcement learning (RL) training on its “latest models intended for deployment” while it tightened up security. The company’s “largest planned frontier RL run remains on hold.”

For its frontier model research, OpenAI now requires stronger sandboxes for workloads that “execute model-generated or otherwise untrusted code,” and has more controls to “isolate higher-risk and untrusted workloads from the internet.” It has also updated its research environment to “remove potentially vulnerable shared services, reduce standing privileges, and improve security and trust boundaries.”

As part of the company’s expanded monitoring setup, OpenAI now aims to issue an alert “within 30 minutes after concerning activity is surfaced,” OpenAI says. If the people paged after an alert can’t “conclusively” determine whether an alert is a false positive within 30 minutes, “those teams are expected to pause the activity.”

OpenAI also says that it’s applying “our core alignment techniques across more stages of the training process,” including reward models that “better detect and discourage unsafe behavior” and training models “to be more honest about their actions, capabilities, and limitations.”

Since the discovery of the Hugging Face breach, Anthropic and Meta have also found that their AI models had hacked other organizations.

Tech.title: PlayStation’s wireless gaming speakers launch in November
Tech.content:
Sony’s Pulse Elevate wireless gaming speakers are launching on November 12th and will cost $219.99, the company announced on Tuesday . Announced nearly a year ago , the speakers are compatible with a PS5, PlayStation Portal, PC, and Mac, and they include “studio-inspired planar magnetic drivers” that offer “lifelike sound across the entire audible spectrum,” Sony says. They also include a built-in mic for voice chat, Sony’s PlayStation Link low-latency tech, and charging docks for topping up the batteries.

The Pulse Elevate speakers come in two colors, black and white, and preorders begin on September 1st at 10AM ET in the US or 10AM local time elsewhere. The black speakers will be available to buy globally on the PlayStation Direct website and at “participating retailers.” The white speakers will only be available on PlayStation Direct in the US, UK, France, Germany, Austria, Belgium, Luxembourg, Netherlands, Italy, Spain, and Portugal, and in other regions at “select” retailers.

Tech.title: Apple squashes EU beef with new App Store rules
Tech.content:
Apple is once again overhauling App Store rules in the European Union, which the company says will resolve its “disagreements with the Commission over business terms and alternative distribution.” As part of the changes, every developer that distributes apps will be moved to a single set of business terms, and digital transactions for apps distributed outside of the App Store will be subject to a Core Technology Commission fee of 5 percent.

The new terms go into effect on October 1st. They will include a 26 percent commission for App Store apps that use Apple’s in-app purchase system, or a 20 percent fee for developers using alternate payment providers. Developers must also pay a 15 percent commission on purchases that link out of the app. Apple will reduce these rates for developers in the App Store Small Business Program, Mini Apps Partner Program, or Video Partner Program.

With the new terms, developers can offer both in-app purchases and alternative payment systems in the EU. However, developers must maintain the payment options they choose for 12 months “to provide consistency and clarity for users,” Apple says.

There’s also a 5 percent Core Technology Commission on digital transactions in apps distributed on third-party app stores and the web. Apple will no longer charge an initial acquisition fee, store services fee, or the Core Technology Fee, a €0.50 per download fee that applied to apps for each annual install over 1 million.

Web distribution is only available in the EU, Apple says, and the company has eligibility requirements in place for who can actually operate a third-party app marketplace over the web, like being a publicly traded company or having completed a financial audit from a “licensed accountant.”

Apple changed its App Store rules last year to comply with the Digital Markets Act (DMA), a set of rules regulating Big Tech. The company has remained critical of the regulations and was fined last year after the Commission found that its App Store “anti-steering” practices violated the DMA. Apple lost its bid to exclude the App Store and iOS from the DMA last month.

Apple’s updates also include new child safety features for the EU. Kids apps in the App Store can’t have links to websites for finishing transactions, and Apple won’t let App Store apps link out to websites for a purchase if a user is under 13 years old. Users under 18 will have to get permission from a parent or guardian when trying to make a purchase using an alternative payment method inside an App Store app.

Tech.title: Tesla is finally launching the Cybercab — let’s hope it’s ready
Tech.content:
is transportation editor with 10+ years of experience who covers EVs, public transportation, and aviation. His work has appeared in The New York Daily News and City & State.

The Tesla Cybercab, that golden two-seater central to Elon Musk’s robo-supremacist ambitions, is finally nearing it’s public launch. Whether or not the no-steering wheel and no-pedal vehicle is actually ready for public roads, let alone customers, remains very much in doubt.

According to The Information, Tesla is planning a public launch of the Cybercab in Austin, Texas, as soon as this month. The driverless vehicle has been popping up around the country, although often with a steering wheel and pedals, as employees are continuing to gather data. Tesla employees have been testing the fully driverless version on private roads around the company’s campus since July. And it recently completed a training with first responders in Austin, teaching them how to move the vehicles in the event of an emergency, Brad Cesak, a spokesperson for the city of Austin, confirmed.

Tesla’s Robotaxi account on X recently confirmed that a “Cybercab launch event” was imminent, inviting followers to take a ride in the company’s Model Y robotaxis in order to win a ticket.

But given what we know about Tesla’s autonomous driving project so far, the Cybercab could be heading for trouble. The Cybercab operates using Tesla’s Full Self-Driving (Supervised) software, which the company claims is significantly safer than human driving. However, independent safety experts and federal regulators have called into question this claim, noting that FSD requires constant driver oversight and remains under active investigation by the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration for traffic compliance failures.

Over a year after its launch, Tesla’s Robotaxi service still uses human safety monitors in some markets. But the Cybercab is designed to operate without any human intervention, which removes one layer of safety on which Tesla can fall back. The company says it employs remote operators who can take control in case of an emergency, but experts question whether signal strength and latency could hamper reactions, especially during incidents in which every second counts. Tesla recently started adding Starlink to its Cybercabs to address this question of connectivity.

There’s also the question of data, and whether Tesla has enough of the right kind. For years, Tesla was assumed to have an advantage in the race to put driverless cars on the road, thanks to the millions of vehicles on the road, passively gathering data to help train its autonomous driving models. But the Cybercab is a different type of vehicle with a unique platform that requires its own specialized data, Musk said during an earnings call in July.

“We need to accumulate driving data that is specific to the Cybercab before we can put a lot of them on the road,” he said.

Once considered to be a leader in data collection, Tesla may actually be a laggard. During that same earnings call, Ashok Elluswamy, the company’s head of AI, said that Tesla’s unsupervised robotaxis have driven 380,000 miles across six cities in two different states. Waymo, which has operated a commercial robotaxi service since 2020, has driven over 220 million fully driverless miles on public roads — or about 579 times more miles than Tesla.

Tesla uses a mix of unsupervised and supervised vehicles as part of its current Robotaxi fleet, but that ratio appears to be in a constant state of flux. According to the crowdsourced Robotaxi Tracker, the company was operating 16 unsupervised vehicles in Austin, four in Dallas, and one in Houston.

Tesla also hasn’t submitted its safety claims for independent analysis, instead relying on self-published statistics while actively working to block public scrutiny of the data it’s required to provide to federal regulators. Meanwhile, Waymo has published several studies in peer-reviewed journals. Recently, the nonprofit Insurance Institute for Highway Safety examined Waymo’s first 50 million miles of fully autonomous driving across multiple cities and concluded that its crash rates were significantly lower than those of human drivers.

The Cybercab launch comes at an odd moment for Tesla. Whereas other vehicle launches have excited Tesla’s many fans with their cutting-edge technology, the Cybercab remains a bit of a curiosity. It’s the lightest, most efficient electric vehicle Tesla has ever produced. But it’s unclear whether the technology powering it is adequate for commercial operations. Still, it’s more like the Tesla Semi than the Model Y or Cybertruck, insofar as it seems destined for commercial service and not personal ownership — despite Musk’s claims that you will eventually be able to buy one.

The Cybercab’s lack of traditional controls means it will be hamstrung by federal safety rules that require things like pedals and side mirrors before they can be sold to the public. That said, if Tesla were to receive an exemption from federal regulators, allowing the company to produce and sell thousands of Cybercabs, that calculus could change. Amazon’s Zoox recently received permission to begin charging for rides in its purpose-built robotaxi. Whether Tesla is also seeking a similar exemption is unknown.

What is known is that Tesla is going to roll out the Cybercab later this month, as if it’s really ready for primetime. But lingering safety questions, as well as the limited nature of Tesla’s Robotaxi service, suggests the Cybercab may still have a long road ahead of it.

Tech.title: Peacock is raising prices by up to $3
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Peacock is raising prices across its streaming plans once again, with the company’s cheapest ad-supported Select tier going from $7.99 to $8.99 / month, as reported earlier by Variety. The Premium plan with ads is increasing from $10.99 to $12.99 / month, while the ad-free Premium Plus plan is getting the biggest hike, jumping from $16.99 to $19.99 / month.

The price change goes into effect on August 18th for new or returning subscribers, and affects the streamer’s annual plans as well. Existing subscribers will see the price change on their next billing date on or after September 17th. Peacock has steadily hiked its prices over the past few years, with the streaming service last issuing a $3 increase in July 2025.

Image: Peacock

On its support page, Peacock says the price change allows the service “to create the best experience for its viewers, remain competitive in the marketplace, and deliver unique content across all genres.” The service has added new features to draw in subscribers, including vertical video for NBA streams, a “Bravoverse” feed with clips from shows like Love Island, and mobile games. It’s also testing perks for long-term subscribers and will soon be included within a YouTube Premium subscription.

NBCUniversal, which owns Peacock, recently reported that the streamer turned a profit for the first time as its subscribers grew to 48 million. Both Peacock and NBCUniversal are preparing to split from Comcast next year.

Tech.title: DOJ’s probe into Andreessen Horowitz over board seats baffles VCs
Tech.content:
The Justice Department has launched a probe into Andreessen Horowitz over the firm’s partners serving on the boards of competing companies, Bloomberg reported.

The nearly year-long investigation focuses specifically on the firm’s board seats at Databricks, which is valued at $190 billion, and Fivetran, which combined with dbt Labs in June. The firm’s co-founder, Ben Horowitz, serves on the board of Databricks, while partner Martin Casado serves on the board of Fivetran.

Several VCs told TechCrunch they were surprised by news of the probe. Databricks and Fivetran are competitors now, but the two companies weren’t rivals when a16z invested in the startups, according to another Databricks investor who spoke on condition of anonymity. Databricks is largely known for its cloud storage products but, with its Lakeflow product, has expanded into AI data pipelines and application connectors. That’s Fivetran’s main business.

Given that Andreessen Horowitz has backed hundreds of companies, it’s almost inevitable that some startups will pivot or expand into the same markets, becoming competitors.

While backing direct rivals has become more acceptable recently, as evidenced by the many VCs that funded both Anthropic and OpenAI, holding a board seat on competing startups creates a far greater conflict of interest. Directors are generally privy to much more sensitive strategic information than non-board investors ever see.

Such conflicts can be resolved by having a partner step down from one of the boards. However, because Databricks and Fivetran have different individuals from the same VC firm on their boards, a16z can institute a so-called Chinese wall between Horowitz and Casado, which would prevent the two partners from sharing confidential information about the two companies with each other, one investor said.

The investigation invokes Section 8 of the Clayton Act, a 112-year-old law stating that an individual or entity is barred from serving on the boards of competing companies. Since regulators have rarely targeted venture capital with this rule, the industry is watching the DOJ’s probe closely. If a16z is forced to surrender a seat, founders may place less value on board commitments from top-tier VCs, given that those investors might be forced to step down if a portfolio overlap creates a future conflict.

a16z did not immediately respond to our request for comment, nor did it respond to Bloomberg. Databricks and DOJ declined comment.

Tech.title: TikTok explores peer-to-peer payments via DMs, report says
Tech.content:
In Brief

TikTok is developing a feature that would allow users to send each other money via direct messages, according to a new report from Bloomberg. If rolled out, the feature would use the social media service’s TikTok Pay offering, which is already available in Southeast Asia for TikTok Shop purchases.

References to the potential feature were found in code hidden within the current version of TikTok’s U.S. iPhone app, according to the report. The code indicates that recipients would be able to “tap to accept” payments, while senders could include messages with their payments, similar to Venmo.

TikTok told Bloomberg that the feature is not being tested, which suggests that it’s in early development. Given that the feature is still under development, it’s unknown when or if TikTok plans to widely release peer-to-peer payments.

TikTok did not immediately respond to TechCrunch’s request for comment.

It’s worth noting that this isn’t the first time TikTok has tried to push further into financial services. Reuters reported earlier this year that TikTok had applied to Brazil’s central bank for approval to operate as a financial technology company offering lending and payment services.

Although TikTok is widely described as a social media giant, it has gradually expanded beyond that category thanks to additions such as robust search, TikTok Shop, a local discovery map, games, hotel bookings, and more. By introducing peer-to-peer payments, TikTok would be competing with services like Venmo and Zelle.

TikTok isn’t the only social network pushing into financial services, as X, formerly known as Twitter, recently launched X Money to allow users to send each other money.

Tech.title: OpenAI institutes new safeguards after Hugging Face breach
Tech.content:
On Tuesday, OpenAI announced a new batch of security policies focused on containing security incidents while models are being tested. The new safeguards include more detailed monitoring of models during the development process, as well as greater emphasis on alignment and security during the post-training process.

“As models become more capable, the risks associated with developing and testing them internally also grow,” the company said in a blog post. “Our standards for monitoring, alignment, and security must stay ahead of those risks.”

The new measures are one of the first public changes in OpenAI’s safety practices since the immediate aftermath of the Hugging Face incident, which was disclosed on July 21.

OpenAI representatives said that the measures are not a direct response to the Hugging Face incident but were also provoked in part by the cybersecurity capabilities of the forthcoming Astra model, as well as the overall pace of progress in AI development.

In the same post, OpenAI disclosed that it had paused reinforcement learning (RL) for two weeks following the Hugging Face incident but had since restarted many of the less-risky models.

“Our largest planned frontier RL run remains on hold while we conduct smaller-scale training and evaluations to assess model behavior, validate our safeguards, and establish more evidence of alignment before proceeding,” the post reads.

Speaking to reporters, OpenAI’s VP of research, Amelia Glaese, emphasized that the strictness of the controls would increase as models became more capable, with the largest models facing the greatest scrutiny.

“We have put in place requirements and expectations for safe development,” Glaese told reporters. “Those requirements and expectations vary with the level of risk that we see.”

OpenAI has been criticized for poor network security practices in the wake of the incident, which saw models escape their training environment by compromising a tool on its network that had access to the internet. The new safeguards include stronger network isolation practices, although the specifics remain vague. Under the new system, the post says, “a single compromise of a workload or supporting service does not, by itself, allow for unauthorized access to the Internet, or other internal networks.”

The strongest safeguard is the monitoring system, which will examine tool actions, available reasoning traces, and activity logs for a variety of unauthorized behavior. OpenAI says it aims to issue alerts within 30 minutes of the concerning activity.

OpenAI estimates that the compute burden of that monitoring will be roughly 20% of whatever process is being monitored. The company promised further details on the system in a forthcoming blog post. The company’s official postmortem analysis of the event is also still pending.
